news.title: Sen. John Thune Wins 2026 Turkey of the Year Award
news.text:
Since the Ringside Politics program began 27 years ago, we have enjoyed an annual tradition. During Thanksgiving week, we announce our “Turkey of the Year” winner. Our previous award recipients have included both celebrities and politicians, as well as Republicans and Democrats.

For example, last year the winner was flamboyant and idiotic Democrat Rep. Jasmine Crockett (TX). In 2024, we bestowed the award on arguably the worst Vice President in American history, the hapless Kamala Harris.

Our 2023 winner was then-Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, the pathetically inept Alejandro Mayorkas, the worst cabinet member of the failed administration of President Joe Biden. He inherited a secure border but created chaos by removing President Donald Trump’s successful policies.

Like these previous winners, our 2026 award winner is a “turkey” in every respect. As usual, this year, we allowed our wonderful audience members to offer their nominations. While many uniquely qualified “turkeys” were nominated, one selection stood out for the 2026 Ringside Politics “Turkey of the Year,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD).

While Thune is technically a Republican, he has been a continual gift to the Democrat Party. Despite Trump calling Thune “a very fine man,” he has been very hostile toward the President’s agenda.

Of the 1,000 bills passed by the U.S. House of Representatives in the last term, “almost 700 still sit untouched in the Senate,” according to GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-MN). The Senate still has not acted on 161 of Trump’s nominations to federal positions, including 25 federal judgeships.

As Senate Majority Leader, Thune led the GOP into the political ditch by refusing to end the filibuster and pass the SAVE America Act, an extremely consequential piece of legislation. The SAVE America Act requires proof of citizenship for voter registration and photo identification to request a mail-in ballot or to vote in person.

Today, only 24 states require photo identification to vote, while 17 states require no identification at all at the polls. Calling this an invitation for fraud is an understatement, and the SAVE America Act would have addressed this gaping loophole in our election system. Unfortunately, Thune showed no interest in passing the legislation despite strong public support.

A Pew Research poll found that an astounding 83 percent of Americans “support requiring some form of government-issued photo ID to vote.” This includes 71 percent of Democrats and 95 percent of Republicans.

The bill was popular with the American people and with President Trump, who continually lobbied for it to pass the Senate, to no avail. He said passing the bill should be the top “priority” for Republicans in 2026. He accurately predicted that if the bill was not passed, Republicans would face “big trouble.”

Indeed, the GOP faced “big trouble” in the 2026 midterms. With the SAVE America Act blocked by Thune, the 2026 midterm elections were not secure, and loyal Republican voters were disillusioned with a party that refused to follow through on major issues. The blame for all of this lies squarely with Thune, a do-nothing Republican leader more interested in keeping good relations with Democrat Party colleagues than in passing crucial legislation to help his party and the country.

This was not the only issue where Thune showed his true political colors. Overall, he is a moderate, not a conservative, and is out of step with a Trump-era Republican Party. His lifetime Heritage Action voting record is an abysmal 64 percent, while the average score for Senate Republicans in the last session is much more respectable, at 88 percent.

Partly because of disillusionment with Thune and other Republicans in Name Only (RINOs) in the Senate, there will be only 44 GOP Senators in the next Congress. Historically, American voters do not reward a party that fails to accomplish anything significant.

As Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) boasted, “56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago. Most people didn't think 51 Democratic Senate seats…a possibility at the beginning of this cycle.” Yet Democrats won their U.S. Senate landslide, taking historic victories in red states once deemed impossible: Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi and Texas.

Losing nine Republican Senators in the midterms is the worst defeat for the GOP since 1958. The next Congress will give Senate Democrats their largest majority since 2010, before the Tea Party revolution brought major wins to the Republican Party.

In athletics, a team with such a losing record would fire its coach, but Senate Republicans did not, as they just re-elected Thune as their Minority Leader. Sen. James Lankford (R-OK) said there was “widespread support” for Thune to remain in his position. Incredibly, Sen. Jim Justice (R-WV) claimed that Thune and his leadership team “didn't cause this problem to happen.” He complimented them for doing “a good job.”

Obviously, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO) was outvoted in the closed-door Republican meeting. He had rightly questioned whether ratifying “all of the same leadership” would send the right message to Republicans. After the monumental Senate Republican losses, Hawley asked those who wanted the same leadership, “I don’t know what planet you’re on.”

Sadly, Sen. Hawley, most of your Senate Republican colleagues prefer to be on a “planet” where they are in the minority and don’t have the burden of leadership. They can complain about Democrats on Fox News, fundraise to Republican donors and, otherwise, enjoy the perks of the “world’s most exclusive club” without having to get anything of significance accomplished.

The epitome of this type of loser mentality is Senator John Thune, who has been in Washington, D.C. for 28 years, far too long. Thune and his long-standing RINO Senate colleagues illustrate why America desperately needs congressional term limits. With leaders like Thune, the GOP will remain in the Senate minority for many years to come.

With such a pitiful, unsuccessful record, it is easy to see why U.S. Senator John Thune was the overwhelming choice for the 2026 Ringside Politics “Turkey of the Year.”

news.title: Fast Takes: Chuck Schumer’s thankless job, gov’t shutdowns hurt average Americans and more
news.text:
From the left: Chuck’s Thankless Job

As progressives push to oust Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader, explains Vox’s Andrew Prokop, realize that the job “isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest,” but “a multitude of tasks” from “crafting legislative and big-picture policy strategy” to “dealing with outside interest groups” and “trying to hold the majority in the next election.” One “underappreciated” key is “volunteering to be the one political figure who’s most likely to be hated,” as were “many of the leaders considered especially effective in their role — from Mitch McConnell to Nancy Pelosi”: Much of what the “base wants can’t happen,” so “many disappointments are inevitable, and that the leader will be the fall guy for them.”

Liberal: Gov’t Shutdowns Hurt Average Americans

“Donald Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran was stupid,” but so “would be provoking a government shutdown in the name of ending the war,” roars the Washington Monthly’s Bill Scher. As the Dec. 11 government funding deadline approaches, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen “has made refusing to fund the war a rallying cry” in his bid to be Dems’ Senate leader. Yet a shutdown would mean “unpaid furloughs for thousands of federal employees two weeks before Christmas,” and a long shutdown could leave “disgusted with both parties for playing political games.” Rather than battling with Trump, Dems can get tangible “affordability” outcomes by focusing on “passing bipartisan tariff reform” instead of being drawn “into another shutdown morass.”

Republican: Democrats’ No. 1 Risk

You can’t fault Democrats for feeling “giddy” after an “election in which they picked up at least 43 House and nine Senate seats,” but The Wall Street Journal’s Karl Rove warns that the “election wasn’t a seismic shift toward Democrats but a rejection of Donald Trump.” Voters “felt he wasn’t focused on rising prices and the economy,” compounded by his “mishandling of immigration enforcement,” “Iran and anger at his self-enrichment schemes.” But Democrats’ energetic “democratic-socialist wing” is “a loser with the broader electorate.” For firebreathing Democrats, “overplaying the oversight card could easily backfire with voters who want more action on inflation and less political infighting.” If they don’t learn from how Trump misread his 2024 win, Democrats “risk misjudging their 2026 victory.”

Eye on ’28: Blacks Key To Ending Dems’ Divides

Analyst Nate Silver “does more than broaden understanding of the intra-Democratic divide,” argues The Washington Post’s Henry Olsen, he “points to the central role that Black voters and leading candidates will play in resolving it.” Silver sees Dems divided on two axes: “ideology and inclination.” It’s the far left vs. the left, but also “fighters (people who want to battle opponents, whether within the party or outside it)” vs. “uniters (those more inclined to find common ground with adversaries).” Blacks are likely the swing bloc, so in the 2028 presidential primaries, watch out for a Black, lefty uniter like ex-Veep Kamala Harris Gov. Wes Moore (Md.) or Sen. Raphael Warnock (Ga.). GOP strategists “salivate at the prospect of” a progressive Democratic nominee; establishment Democrats prefer a “unifying moderate” — but: Don’t be surprised if the eventual nominee, drawing on strong support from Black voters, splits the difference.”

Conservative: Media Touts Fake Sanctions Expert

“The commentary of a ‘sanctions expert,’ Brett Erickson,” emerged “around the start of the Iran War” and appeared in “media outlets around the country,” widely cited “expounding on how the Iranians were likely to outgun President Donald Trump at every twist and turn of the war, and otherwise “slamming the administration,” reports The Free Beacon’s Eliana Johnson. Yet he’s a 29-year-old with “little professional expertise” in the areas of “financial crime and geopolitics” for which he claims to be an expert. He “has amassed a litany of impressive-sounding credentials” by paying for “online certifications” without “ever actually working in the area”; he claims to be the principal of a company, but its main office “is registered at a single-family home in Arizona.” 

— Compiled by The Post Editorial Board
news.summary: As progressives push to oust Chuck Schumer as Senate Democratic leader, explains Vox’s Andrew Prokop, realize that the job “isn’t really about winning a national popularity contest.”

news.title: Ossoff's broad and decisive Senate win fuels 2028 speculation
news.text: Washington — Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding reelection victory in Georgia is drawing renewed attention to his potential as a 2028 presidential contender, as election data shows how he assembled a broad coalition of voters in the pivotal presidential battleground state.Despite the growing speculation, Ossoff, 39, is for now dismissing the possibility of a White House bid. During a debate in October, Ossoff said he had "zero interest in running for president" in 2028.Some early polls place him at the top of a hypothetical 2028 primary field. A post-election Emerson College survey showed Ossoff with the support of 17% of respondents — narrowly ahead of former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and California Gov. Gavin Newsom rounding out the top five. Ossoff has attracted interest from both centrists and progressives while delivering a decisive victory in a closely divided presidential battleground state. At Crooked Con, a primarily progressive gathering in Washington after the midterms, Ossoff received 38% of first-choice votes in its straw poll, ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg."I think he would make an attractive presidential contender on the Democratic side," said Jerry Gonzalez, CEO of GALEO Impact Fund PAC, a Georgia-based Latino political action committee that endorsed Ossoff in his Senate race. "He is not afraid, he won't shy away from holding the Trump administration accountable, but in a way that works towards actually building coalitions to get something done." Democrats who can win statewide in conservative or swing states tend to be moderate, and that's true of Ossoff, too. "He comes across, and tries to present himself, as a moderate, and he talks about issues which moderate conservatives could get behind," said Charles Bullock, a longtime political science professor at the University of Georgia. "The issues he stresses are things which are within the broad mainstream of 'These would be good things.'"It's unclear how well a moderate would fare in the early nominating states. What is effective in a Georgia general election may be a tougher sell in a Democratic primary, where voters often reward ideological purity over swing-state caution. "Obviously, he's successful here in Georgia," Bullock said. "How would he play elsewhere? "I think what we will be seeing is preparation, maybe for a later run," Bullock speculated. Ossoff's record gives rivals on both flanks openings to attack: progressives have criticized his vote for the Republican-backed Laken Riley Act and his reluctance to embrace "Medicare for All," while his votes to restrict certain weapons sales to Israel and his criticism of its military conduct in Gaza have drawn objections from some pro-Israel Democrats and donors.All of those issues are certain to be part of the 2028 primary contest. For example, Rep. Ro Khanna, another potential 2028 candidate, last week tried to restart the debate over universal healthcare. "Medicare for All means healthcare for everyone, like public school is free for every kid," Khanna wrote on X, arguing, "'Medicare for All who want it' is pablum. It's telling parents they have to pay for public school." In his reelection this month, Ossoff defeated GOP opponent Mike Collins by around 18 points, two years after President Trump defeated Harris by around two points in 2024. It was a much wider margin than his last Senate election, which he won by just over one percentage point.Powering Ossoff's win this year was a broad coalition of voters, including some swing constituencies that Democrats have struggled with in recent years, CBS News' exit polling shows.Ossoff maintained strong support among Black voters, winning 93% of the group, which make up almost one-third of the state's eligible voters according to Pew Research Center.He did not win the White voters who make up just over half of Georgia's electorate, but he did make significant inroads, winning 40% — after Harris had won just 28% two years earlier. He also notched some improvement in groups that have shifted hard against Democrats: He won 29% of White voters without college degrees (compared to Harris' 18%) and 19% of White evangelical or born-again Christian voters (compared to less than 10% for Harris).Ossoff also won men by nine points after Harris lost them by 13 points.Both Ossoff and Harris won younger Georgians, but Ossoff won them by a larger margin, securing 85% of voters ages 29 and under. Ossoff also split the 45-and-older vote roughly in half, while Harris lost that age group by a 15-point margin.And Ossoff made gains with Hispanics — a group that makes up less than 10% of Georgia's eligible voters but which has grown rapidly and has become a swing demographic that could decide a close race in the perennial battleground. In his reelection victory, he won around two-thirds of Latino voters, up seven points from Harris' performance two years earlier.A comparison of 19 Georgia precincts where at least 30% of active registered voters identify as Hispanic or Latino shows substantial Democratic improvement.Ossoff won those precincts by a combined 49 points in the two-candidate vote, compared with an eight-point advantage for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and an 18-point margin for fellow Democratic Sen. Raphael Warnock in 2022.The changes were significant in areas that had supported Mr. Trump just two years earlier.In six heavily Latino precincts in Whitfield County, the combined results shifted from a 12-point Trump advantage in 2024 to a 37-point Ossoff victory in 2026. Three similar precincts in Hall County shifted from an 11-point Trump edge to a 33-point Ossoff victory.Those figures reflect the voting behavior of entire precincts rather than individual Latino voters, and comparisons between presidential and midterm electorates are not exact. Still, they underscore how dramatically the environment changed in places with large Latino populations.Gonzalez attributed the shift in part to concerns over affordability and immigration enforcement, two issues he said weighed heavily on Latino voters in Georgia."Things are really expensive," Gonzalez told CBS News. "The price and affordability were a big driving issue." He also pointed to the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and its impact on Latino communities in Georgia. Ossoff has investigated allegations of abuses in federal immigration detention facilities as part of his Senate oversight work.Gonzalez also credited Ossoff's success among voters across the political spectrum to his accessibility and constituent outreach. "His office is accessible to all Georgians, and that's part of the reason why he won."In this wave election, Ossoff wasn't the only Democrat to pick up ground in the midterms. Latino and Black voters, men, voters without college degrees and younger voters moved back toward Democratic candidates nationwide, a reversal after all four groups had shifted rightward in 2024.In 2028, those groups could once again play a central role in both the Democratic Party's nominating process and the general election.States with large Black and Latino populations will lead the Democratic primary calendar after the party rearranged its schedule, and Ossoff, with his strong support from both groups, would likely stand to benefit if he were to decide to run. South Carolina — where Black Democratic voters have long played an influential role in choosing the party's presidential nominee — will go first, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan and Virginia.The DNC says approximately 4.2 million Latinos live across the six early nominating states, a major increase from the party's previous early-state lineup.In the general election, maintaining a strong lead with Black, Latino and younger voters — and preventing too much slippage among White and non-college-educated voters — will also be a core task for Democrats, as they seek to prevent the GOP's first non-Trump presidential candidate in over a decade from reassembling the Trump coalition.Though Ossoff says he doesn't plan a White House bid in 2028, his performance in Georgia has provided an early measure of what an electoral coalition for him could look like."He has mentioned that he was focused on winning reelection, which he has done, so I think that gives him a little bit of latitude to think about it a little more seriously," Gonzalez said.
news.summary: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff's commanding victory in Georgia relied on a broad coalition, and this is fueling 2028 presidential interest in him, even though he says he'll be in the Senate for the next six years.
news.author: Joe Walsh,Zak Hudak

news.title: PRedictions, PRojections, PRaise, and PRedators: The 5 Mistakes That Lost the Midterms
news.text:
A dyslexic approach to problem-solving, where we begin with the ending and work our way back, is actually how PR pros build marketing plans: We figure out where the brand wants to be — and then we plot our path backwards. The better we can describe the ending, the better our plan.

‘Cause that’s all a marketing plan is: a roadmap between two points.

And so are post-election autopsies. You start with the death, pinpoint the mortal wounds, and then reverse-engineer what the hell happened. 

Let’s apply this to the 2026 midterms. After all, we already know where we are: on the wrong side of a landslide. Even if you figured we’d lose (I predicted we’d lose the House and Senate), the size and scope of the blue wave caught everyone off guard — including the Democrats. They didn’t think they’d sweep Texas, Maine, Mississippi, Michigan, Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina, and Alaska, either.

(Nor did I. I figured the House was toast and the Senate was almost certainly kaput, but the GOP would win at least a few of the battleground races. Instead, we were shut out completely, and now the Senate is 56-44 Democrat.)

So what were the five biggest mistakes that led to the GOP’s drubbing?

Since a mistake is the byproduct of a decision, I’m not going to include what’s arguably the biggest reason that Republicans lost: historical headwinds. 

The truth is, it’s exceedingly improbable for the in-power party to win a midterm election, and if Kamala Harris had won in 2024, there wouldn’t have been a blue wave.

If anything, the wave would’ve been red.

No more stalling. Here’s the list:

Honorable mention: Deaths of Renée Nicole Good (Jan. 7, 2026) and Alex Jeffrey Pretti (Jan. 24, 2026)

It was less the deaths themselves than what these deaths symbolized: President Donald Trump and the Republican Party lost the PR image war in the immigration debate. What once was Trump’s strongest issue was negated by bad press, bad execution, and partisan blowback. It helped energize Democratic activism, outrage, and turnout.

Only the ham-fisted GOP could turn one of the most remarkable success stories in government history — securing our border, lowering crime and drug deaths, and saving 50,000 American lives — into a political albatross! (It’s morbidly impressive.)

Part of the blame belongs to Kristi Noem. She turned out to be an abysmal cabinet selection (and the bizarreness of the homeland secretary’s home life wasn’t exactly helpful either). Part of the blame belongs to the Republican Party, for failing to help the American people connect the dots between a secure border, lower crime, safer streets, and fewer addicts dying.

But when you’re the president, the buck stops with you. From the top-down, the immigration debate was botched from the get-go.

And now, the top five…

Number Five: Tariff Day, a.k.a. “Liberation Day” (April 2, 2025)

Post-Trump, it’s unclear if the Republican Party will be a pro-tariff party. In many ways, it’s an unnatural fit for the party of limited government. Tariffs appeal to isolationists (and quite a few realists), mostly because other countries cheat at trade and/or manipulate the rules. Without protectionist policies, they argue, American jobs will vanish.

The purpose of this column isn’t to advocate for or against tariffs. I’m simply reporting the political reality: Americans blame tariffs for the so-called “affordability crisis.”

Which is why it hurt us on Election Day.

In fact, for all the handwringing about the Iran War, more Americans blamed President Trump’s tariff policies than the Iran War for higher prices:

More voters blame Trump's tariffs for raising cost of living than Iran war: poll https://t.co/NTyaiPKa4d https://t.co/xTN6xFQC8m— New York Post (@nypost) November 19, 2026

Some track his decline in the polls to “Liberation Day”:

The Woke Right, who actually have been pushing this stuff in the White House, are desperate to make sure people don't recognize this simple truth. They have seemingly known it all along too. Trump inherited a country that just suffered high inflation and other reasons for high prices, and people wanted economic stability and improvement. The logic, if not just post-liberal stupidity, is that this kind of economic protectionism would drive manufacturing back to the U.S. and, inexplicably, level out trade deficits, as if that's some kind of a goal for the holder of the world's reserve currency. While a little of that happened, I don't think tariffs would work even in the long term for the goals they were seeking, but even if they would have, they wouldn't work in two years. They kept prices high and caused a lot of ancillary problems across the board. Tariffs are expensive, and autarky (economic self-sufficiency) is also expensive. That means goods and services are expensive. The graphs of approval ratings for Trump clearly show a negative trajectory from the day he imposed them, which he also inexplicably called "Liberation Day." In my opinion, the Trump administration overall, and Trump himself, own this mistake and should correct it. I know post-liberal idiots like Oren Cass, a close advisor and friend of JD Vance, and his American Compass outfit were instrumental in keeping them going, so they should probably eat more of the blame, but Trump wears these himself too. Period. But, the Woke Right took advantage of these high prices and even maintained inflationary rates to blame the Iran War for the prices the second that it started. They blamed nothing else. Iran closing Hormuz made this explanation stick like glue, and the graph shows another incredible tanking of approval that correlates to it. The thing is, it's not the war that raised the prices. That was always malicious propaganda, serving New Right, Russian, and Iranian interests (no coincidence that it's all of these at once). The war became the bogus primary explanation for high prices when, in fact, it was a modest increase. The wicked New Right, Russia, and Iran would have understood all of this, that they could pin the high prices that were largely a combination of the legacy of Bidenflation plus the way Trump's (and Vance-Cass's) tariffs scheme maintained those high prices and inflation rates. The war was big, obvious, and visible, so of course it made things more expensive, or so the logic goes. In truth, things were expensive mostly for other reasons, including the stupid tariffs, and the propaganda turned people against Trump over the war. Now, the New Right, along with Russia and Iran, no doubt, are pushing the line as hard as possible that the war, largely because of affordability concerns, was the primary driver in losing the midterms, which is also starkly out of step with any real, sober analysis (many other factors weigh heavily, not least the tariffs and their economic consequences). There are many reasons for this. One, it allows Vance's people to target their enemies in the administration effectively by blaming the war and thus those who supported it, especially Trump, Hegseth, and Rubio. A lot of that will be successful, even though it's grotesque, malicious, and false. Two, I'm not saying they have deals with the Russians or Iranians or are doing their bidding, but... I didn't say that. Three, it allows them to keep anger about the war high and to leverage to pull out of it, which serves... Russian and Iranian, if not also Chinese, interests most. The New Right also depends on this anger to mobilize its infantile base. Four, autarky is always expensive and therefore has to be propped up by "nationalist" policy that they want to force on people, so these bad policies become a lever to accomplish their worse policies. Five, it allows them to maintain their "nationalist" push for autarkic policy (high tariffs) even though they're the main cause of the problem, which fits with their "nationalist" (national socialist...) agenda along with Russia/China's Dugin-driven "multipolarity" theory, which requires an isolated America ("America First"). Six, repeating that last one for emphasis: it lets them keep doing the stupid tariffs, which they want for bad reasons that run a fairly wide gamut, none of which are genuinely in American interests. I don't know if there's corruption there they're profiting from (I guarantee there is), or if that's how these foreign entities that benefit so much from their policies might be controlling them (...), but it's a decent bet, too. Which is like a seventh reason: they have to because they're compromised through their own crooked deal-making. At any rate, the tariffs were not a good policy. If the proposed mechanism was going to work, it wouldn't work in the time allotted, and it is unlikely that they'd actually work (autarky is always expensive and requires a lot of "nationalist" policy to keep it going). Nonetheless, the New Right (and its foreign alignments) ran an extremely successful propaganda campaign that they are now accelerating vigorously to lead people to the wrong conclusions and to dramatically undercut Republicans (so they can leverage that to try to take over the party with more bad ideas).— James Lindsay, anti-Communist (@ConceptualJames) November 6, 2026

Perhaps tariffs are a necessary evil; perhaps they’re self-destructive and foolhardy. (Believe whatever you want.) But in 2026, they were politically hurtful. Thems the facts, bro.

In an election where the #1 issue was affordability, tariffs were a high-visibility scapegoat.

Number Four: Pam Bondi’s Epstein Files (mis)release (Feb. 27, 2025) and Elon Musk posting on X that Trump “is in the Epstein Files” (June 5, 2025)

The irony is, the Biden administration stonewalled the release of the Epstein Files; President Trump was the one who shared them with the public.

But when ex-Attorney General Pam Bondi overpromised and underdelivered, the blowback was extraordinary. She promised scandalous new info — tens of thousands of hours of shocking video footage — yet delivered tired old news. 

It was catnip for the tin-hat crowd. Suddenly, everyone was talking about Jeffrey Epstein. 

This was the beginning of the drip-drip-drip.

Then, on June 5, Elon Musk threw a temper tantrum over the Big Beautiful Bill and posted one of the most damaging, ill-advised statements in social media history. He’s since deleted it, but the internet never forgets:

“Time to drop the really big bomb: @realDonaldTrump is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public. Have a nice day, DJT!” https://t.co/j0v472W0Fg— WBTV News (@WBTV_News) June 7, 2025

“Epstein Class” became shorthand for government corruption, unaccountable billionaires, Donald Trump’s friends, and businessmen with suspiciously Semitic-sounding names. The one-two punch of Bondi’s bungling and Musk’s X post elevated a side-issue into an ongoing distraction, and Epstein isn’t going away in 2027.

The House Democrats are calling for a special counsel to investigate Trump’s ties to Epstein. And now that they control Congress, they’ll get what they want. All the way through, the Epstein debacle is a textbook example of what NOT to do in crisis communications.

We literally handed the Dems a club to beat us over the head.

Number Three: GOP legislative incompetence, especially the SAVE Act (June 4, 2026)

Actually, the SAVE Act failed quite a few times. It passed the House in April of 2025 yet never advanced in the Senate. The revised SAVE Act passed the House in February of 2026 and then failed to overcome the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster.

Then, it failed twice in the Senate, including on June 4, losing 48-50 both times. Republican Senators Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Mitch McConnell, and Thom Tillis all voted against it.

This was a life-and-death issue for the GOP base. Few issues mattered to us more. Watching it crash and burn was painful.

It demotivated Republican turnout. This was the GOP’s opportunity to give us a reason to vote FOR them. 

But instead of delivering, they gave the base the finger.

Lots of us voted anyway, but we really weren’t voting for the Republicans anymore. All we had left was voting against the Democrats.

If you want to know why Republicans were slaughtered in the enthusiasm gap, the death of the SAVE Act is a great place to start!

(And, of course, if you’re suspicious of the Democrats’ dramatic jump in midterm turnout, the absence of the SAVE Act is — at least for some — potential evidence of untrustworthy results. Which isn’t healthy for democracy, either.)

Number Two: The Iran War (Feb. 28, 2026) and the Iran MOU (June 17, 2026)

Some blame the Iran War, some blame the Iran MOU. I’m gonna split the difference and blame ‘em both.

Because they both point to the same problem: an unsatisfactory conclusion.

President Trump insists he did the right thing, and perhaps his decision will be well-received in time. But the immediate impact was detrimental: It spiked gas prices right before the midterm, it divided elements of the MAGA movement, and this on-again, off-again Schrödinger’s cat of a conflict lacked a clear, convincing victory.

It also became a wedge issue for Israel-bashers to exploit. If you’re a Zionist voter, the Iran War might’ve saved millions of people from a nuclear holocaust, but it further damaged Israel’s reputation in the West. (I’m not saying this with a smile on my face; I’m just calling balls and strikes.)

Without the Iran War, Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign would’ve lost its go-to whipping horse. The war itself — and the sputtering way we prosecuted it — hurt the Republican Party. 

Either in conception or implementation, we screwed the pooch. (Politically, at least.)

Number One: The murder of Charlie Kirk (Sept. 10, 2025)

His death wasn’t a “mistake” — it was a deliberate, preplanned crime. Calling it a mistake lets Tyler Robinson, the alleged murderer, skate culpability.

But allowing his death to divide the MAGA movement? That was a yuuuuge mistake. 

It’s one we still haven’t recovered from.

The first tragedy was the murder itself. Charlie was just 31; he left behind a wife and two children. Our heart aches for all of them.

The second tragedy was how MAGA reacted. Because, under different circumstances, this could’ve been the moment we rallied together, realized that the people who killed Charlie would’ve happily killed any of us, and dedicated ourselves to honoring Charlie’s life.

Instead, his murder became fodder for moronic conspiracies. Sleaze-merchants monetized his name for YouTube views. His widow and his children were exploited — over and over again — for clicks.

I don’t have access to Candace Owens’ finances, but I wouldn’t be surprised if she made millions by desecrating Charlie Kirk’s memory.

And she’s not alone. Tucker Carlson and others have repeatedly evoked his memory to link him to causes he never supported, including antisemitism, hatred of Israel, and support of Islam.

As a result, our movement has splintered. We spent much of the last year fighting with ourselves.

Meanwhile, the Democrats were so unified against all-things MAGA, the DSA and the Democratic establishment were working together.

news.title: Sunday Smiles
news.text:
One of my guilty pleasures in life is reading Nellie Bowles' TGIF column every Friday. 

I usually don't get around to it until my writing for the day is done, and sometimes not until the weekend is in full swing, but it is my version of Sunday Smiles. 

Nellie is funny, and while she is not quite as cynical as I am, she comes close, and from a different angle because she is female, a lesbian, a mother, and fairly liberal. 

You'd never guess, but I don't overlap much with her in the Venn Diagram of life. 

Still, that shared cynicism creates a significant overlap in the humor regions of the brain, and she often notices the same things as I do when it comes to systems not working as described. 

For example:

→ Our underfunded schools: New York City’s public school population is down 21.5 percent since 2013. Yes, it’s fallen by a fifth as families with young children flee the city to find schools that teach their kids forbidden knowledge like math and reading. People suffer miserable commutes and deal with things like lawn care and carpooling because the alternative is a man-child communist telling their children that America is satanic while a kid twirls a handgun one desk over. Anyway, school enrollment is down 21.5 percent. But funding is up! Oh yeah it is. New York City now spends $59,450 per student! Per year! That’s the number people are arriving at because the city’s public school budget this year is now $45.6 billion. For only 766,900 students. This is the math they don’t want you to do. $59,450. For that price, these kids should be speaking Mandarin while they code a new internet. For nearly 60 grand, those kids should be able to land back handsprings on the moon. Sixty grand should mean the kid has some alternative thoughts on Russian literature.

Now if I had written about that, it would have been a screed, because screeds are what I do best. But when Nellie makes fun of it, I have to chuckle along with her, because, once you get past the fact that countless idiots nod along when teachers' unions and liberal politicians keep raising taxes because "schools are underfunded," it really IS funny that people keep buying the bulls**t and applauding when they do. 

The consequences are awful: kids' lives are ruined, people who can't afford private schools but who can afford to move do, and the Democratic Socialists of America get new voters because the next generation has the intellectual development of toddlers, but if you look at it just right, you see the humor. 

Dark, cynical humor, but then so much humor is dark and cynical. You have to laugh, or you would be crying all the time, and what is the point of that? 

Many memes are dark and cynical too. Sometimes you have to laugh, because it is a better alternative than raging.

news.title: Biden's memoir lauds his record but skirts Gaza and re-election errors
news.text: By Jennifer Szalai PROMISE ME, AMERICAby Joe BidenPublished by Little, Brown465 pages $42 Joe Biden wants you to know that he is proud of himself — and if his new memoir is any indication, he thinks everyone else should be proud of him, too. Promise Me, America begins with soaring declarations about the “long sweep of history” and the “fundamental goodness” of the United States (US), before turning into a minutely detailed account of his presidential accomplishments. The result reads like a mix of cover letter and campaign speech — one that’s more than 400 pages long. It didn’t have to be this way. The post-presidential memoir is an uneven genre; to engage in sustained reflection requires some humility, a quality for which former presidents aren’t typically known. And Biden, who turns 84 on November 20, can legitimately lay claim to a raft of domestic policy feats at an extraordinarily difficult time. Pandemic relief, infrastructure, clean energy, semiconductor manufacturing: He understandably wants to chronicle the hard work behind these achievements, and more. But enumerating the wins is easy. The true test of a book like this is whether its author will own his losses, too. Biden, for his part, does not. He is so preoccupied with burnishing his legacy that he gets awkward and defensive when addressing the two issues many readers will be most curious about: his handling of the war in Gaza, and his decision to run for a second term. From the first chapter, “History Comes Knocking”, the book runs on two tracks: steady pragmatism and accelerating grandiosity. Biden takes pains to show how, as a 78-year-old commander in chief, he assembled a “great team”, and he is plenty willing to give credit where credit is due. Not that the book’s trajectory is ever in doubt. It begins on January 6, 2021, when Trump supporters stormed the Capitol. It ends with Trump back in power. When announcing his run for a second term, Biden says, he chose to emphasise that his opponent was a threat to democracy: “He said he’d be a dictator on Day 1. He was planning to invoke the Insurrection Act, which would allow him to deploy troops on the streets of America. He was calling those who opposed him ‘vermin’. He talked about the ‘blood’ of America as being ‘poisoned’, echoing the language used in Nazi Germany.” Why, then, did Trump win? Biden has his ideas. His own policies, he argues, couldn’t have had anything to do with it. (Regarding Kamala Harris, he “was proud of her and the campaign she ran”.) He decided to run again because he “wanted to finish the job”. In addition to describing his legislative victories, the book includes an appendix to hammer this point home. “Laws Signed by President Joseph R Biden Jr.” lists a “selection” of the “more than 600 bills” he signed into law. As for his age and his health, he repeatedly contends that these weren’t a problem either. He believes that Americans supported him, casting a primary win in New Hampshire as “a resounding vote of confidence”. Instead, he blames “the press and pundits” for pushing a “narrative” and “salivating” at the prospect of his humiliation. “Yes, people could point to moments when I mixed up names or lost my train of thought or had a weak voice or walked slowly,” he writes, grudgingly. “But they could never point to something presidential that I failed to do.” Even he cannot wholly disavow his abysmal debate performance against Trump in 2024, and so he shrugs it off as no big deal. “Lots of presidents had bad debates,” he says, pointing to Barack Obama’s first debate against Mitt Romney. “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me.” The sulking at the end of that quote is telling. Biden’s voice gets passive; he portrays himself as the helpless victim of events. He gets similarly defensive when recounting the war in Gaza. “I repeatedly sought to restrain the Israelis,” he says, citing multiple instances when he gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a stern talking-to amid the escalating Palestinian death toll. Reassessing America’s unconditional military aid to Israel was apparently out of the question. Biden offers no explanation why, other than to say that he had “always felt an affinity” for the country. Biden maintains he would have “prevailed” at the 2024 Democratic National Convention. He says he eventually relented to pressure and bowed out of the race for the sake of “party unity”. In May 2025, he learned he had Stage 4 prostate cancer. He mentions this in his epilogue, though he says nothing about how such a development could have affected him and presumably the country had he gotten his way and been granted another go as president. You have to marvel at such formidable powers of compartmentalisation: Biden still wants us to know that he could have won. The reviewer is the nonfiction book critic for The Times

news.title: James Carville Warns Democrats They Risk Losing Power Over a Choice Looming Ahead
news.text:
On a recent episode of his Politics War Room podcast, famed Democrat strategist James Carville laid out a rather interesting choice his party may soon face, and he didn't hesitate to make it. If Democrats have to pick between black voters and white urban lefties, Carville wants them to go with the black voters.

Now, I've been mocking Carville a lot lately, and he's earned every bit of mockery he can get. His Trump Derangement Syndrome is off the charts. He used to be a smart strategist, but he's become too poisoned by hatred to see anything objectively.

Take the 2024 election. Carville literally guaranteed that Kamala Harris would beat Donald Trump. Sure, there were a lot of people on the left who thought she'd win, but Carville went further and guaranteed it. Why? Because his hatred of Trump was so rabid that he was completely blind to what was actually going on with the electorate that year. The man who coined the phrase “it’s the economy, stupid” didn’t realize that the economy sucked and voters wanted change.

So you'd expect his latest analysis to be more of the same. Of course, it isn't, and that's what makes it worth a closer look.

Mark McKinnon, a former adviser to President George W. Bush, joined the podcast and opened the topic by referring to something Carville had told him off-air. "James, you said something to me before we started the program that really caught my attention, which is you think that the progressive left has, I don't know how you describe it, a misunderstanding, insensitivity to black voters in general," McKinnon said. "Can you go deeper on that?"

Carville noted that the far left likes to lump marginalized groups from around the world into one big coalition. Then he explained where black Americans depart from that project.

"Black people by and large view themselves as having a very unique problem," Carville said. "And that is, well, they're black and they have a different history or an entirely different history. They are aware of their history. All right."

He then warned his party against confusing good manners with agreement, a mistake Democrat activists make constantly when they assume a polite audience is a persuaded one. "And they don't want to be, they're not going to be rude to anybody," he continued. "But if you come to them from Seattle and start talking this progressive nonsense, you're not going to go anywhere. And it's very important to understand that."

Carville reached back to his roots in Louisiana politics for the next part. "Me growing up in Southern politics, growing up in Democratic politics, there is no more important voting constituency, no more wild voting constituency in a Democratic party than black people are, period, in the memo," he said. "And if you ask me, we got to jettison these urban a** whites or we got to jettison black folks, that is not a very hard question for me to answer."

For our VIPs: Why Are Democrats So Beholden to the Trans Cult?

"All right. Exit stage left, urban progressive a**holes," Carville added. "I'm going to dance with the folks that brought me here."

I can’t imagine that strategists make a habit of proposing to cut loose part of their own coalition for fun. Black voters have long been the Democrat Party's most dependent bloc, routinely delivering margins of 80 or 90 points. Shave even a few points off those numbers, and Democrats start losing more races in key states. Carville knows the math.

So when a man this consumed by hatred of Trump starts urging Democrats to ditch white voters in favor of black voters, it means he knows Democrats are at risk of losing black voters. He sees a true problem for his party, and it's serious enough to break through even his blinders.

The reason Carville is saying this is obvious. Under Trump, there has been a significant shift in the black vote, and Trump made huge gains with black voters. Yes, they swung back to Democrats in the 2026 midterms, but the GOP has proven it can win them back, and Carville understands that. Democrats have spent decades treating black voters as a guaranteed asset, and Carville just admitted the guarantee has expired.

news.title: Guest columnist Max Page: Tax the rich. Fund public education. Win elections.
news.text:
One of Wallace Steven’s most famous poems is “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird.” I’ve come back repeatedly to the fifth stanza:

I do not know which to prefer,The beauty of inflectionsOr the beauty of innuendoes,The blackbird whistlingOr just after. 

We just had an election of monumental importance. And now the stories get told about what it meant. The election was the “inflection.” What we make of it is the “innuendo.”

The poet insists he does “not know which to prefer.” In politics, we have no choice but to look forward, to tell the story and to shape the “innuendoes.”

One key lesson from the beautifully unexpected repudiation of President Donald Trump and his lapdog enablers in the Party of Trump and in the billionaire class is that fighting to retake the country from the wealthy in order to fund public education, a core common good, is a recipe for electoral victory.

Look at the shocking victories in Texas. Gina Hinojosa, who will be the first Latina governor in the history of Texas, was inspired to run, and made as a foundation of her campaign, the fight for public schools. She beat Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seen as unbeatable only days before the election. James Talarico was a public school teacher who built his reputation in the Texas legislature as a defender of public education and became an outspoken opponent of Abbott and the Republican Party’s decimation of public education through private school vouchers and public school funding cuts. 

Dozens of other candidates in states across the country made investing in public education— and protecting it from private school voucher schemes that are designed to crush the very idea of universal, free, public education — a key plank. The Prop 3 referendum to make permanent a tax on millionaires to fund public education passed almost 60-40 in California. Meanwhile, the Prop 40 California wealth tax, which was focused on protecting healthcare, was opposed by the $300 million of a few billionaires, suffered from a lack of funds and division in the labor coalition, and ultimately failed.

Washington voters soundly rejected an attempt by the very rich to roll back the millionaire’s tax, modeled on our own Fair Share Amendment, which will benefit public education. Here in Massachusetts, we rejected the second of two attempts to undermine the Fair Share Amendment, the 2024 amendment to our Constitution that is bringing in over $3 billion a year from the wealthiest residents of the commonwealth. Those efforts were led by the Mass High Tech Council, Pioneer Institute and Competitiveness Council. They resent that we, the citizens of Massachusetts, are “calling back,” in the words of our Amherst permanent poet laureate, Emily Dickinson, about $3 billion a year to fund everything from more childcare, to universal school meals, to free higher education and better roads and bridges and public transportation. One of those efforts was thrown out by the Supreme Judicial Court, the other by the voters on Nov. 3.

And this is hardly new. Look back to the 2024 election. In Kentucky, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 30 points. But those same voters, on the same ballot, voted by the exact same margin to reject private school vouchers. In Nebraska, where Trump won about 60% of the vote, vouchers were rejected 57-42. You can’t achieve that result unless many of the voters who voted to return Trump to the White House also rejected one of his and the Republicans’ central — and maybe their only — public education policy: diverting public money to private and religious schools. 

When I was president of the Massachusetts Teachers Association and traveling almost daily up to Gloucester during the educator strike (which was illegal in Massachusetts, incidentally) in November 2024, I was struck by a house at the bottom of the off-ramp from Route 1. On one column of the front porch was a MAGA “Make America Great Again” sign. And on the other column was a sign with this message: “Support the Union of Gloucester Educators.” People can gravitate toward conservative candidates who appear populist, but they care deeply about the public schools and public school educators to which they entrust their children. 

And they want to tax the very rich, to take back some of their ungodly power to purchase elected officials and policies that benefit the rich and to invest in the things voters care about, most centrally public education. A recent poll by Hart Research, which was commissioned by Better Taxes for a Better America, found that 85% of voters felt that the wealthy should be taxed more. That number beat out the response to questions about whether or not the Earth is round and if apple pie is tasty. In other words, we have a near-universal consensus that the wealthy need to pay their fair share, as long as the money is invested in what matters most, and public education is at the top of the list. 

We are at an inflection point. Let the “innuendoes” from this election make their way into the public policy platforms of 2028 and beyond.

Max Page is a professor of architecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

news.title: Report: AOC and Kamala Harris Are the 'X-Factor' in the 2028 Presidential Primary Contest
news.text:
With the midterms only a few weeks in the rearview mirror attention has already turned to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary, where one news outlet reported it was ready “to explode into sprawling, wide-open field.”

That was the conclusion of an NBC News analysis on Saturday of the contest two years away, with the network pointing out that anyone with a notion of running for president first must navigate the presence of high-profile Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) and former VP and failed 2024 candidate Kamala Harris.

As NBC described the challenge:

Both are known universally within their party, have demonstrated the ability to raise ungodly sums of money and rank at or near the top in early polls — standards that most presidential hopefuls will never achieve.
And both take up commanding lanes of the electorate. Harris, the former vice president, won 75 million votes as the party’s nominee in 2024 and 92% of Black women voters. Ocasio-Cortez, a congresswoman from New York, is widely perceived to be the heir to the progressive populist movement built by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

Yet, neither women have expressed their intentions for 2028, which looms as an “X factor” for other potential candidates as they begin to devise their campaign strategies.

“It fundamentally changes the dynamics of the primary. They are the ones sitting on the biggest blocs,” veteran Democratic pollster Celinda Lake told NBC. “They have total name recognition. Despite all the controversies — they are actually well-liked by key constituencies of a Democratic primary.”

Lake has polled in the past for Ocasio-Cortez. She said both women candidates would generate a “fundamental reshuffling of the coalitions, of the targeting strategies, of the themes, of what people will be looking for, who is considered viable and not.”

RELATED: The Return of Rambling Kamala

The network apparently surveyed more than 20 Democratic “strategists, pollsters and elected officials” who pointed out any candidate faced a “minefield” if Cortez or Harris launch campaigns. They also said that if neither funs, the competition will be to win their endorsements.

Lake pointed out that Harris’ popularity with Black women makes her an immediate threat, particularly in the influential South Carolina primary early in the nomination calendar. Harris has been coy about her intentions, as she was about running for California governor, which she ultimately declined to do.

Just elected to a fifth term in the House, Ocasio-Cortez has not ruled out a bid for the presidency but is also exploring a run in 2028 for the New York Senate seat currently occupied by Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.

If both women stay out of the race, NBC reported, it could leave the field without a female candidate, though Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) has expressed an interest in running.

According to exit polling, the midterm wins were generated by woman, with 60 percent of female voters supporting the Democratic choices on the ballot.

RELATED: JD Vance Roasts AOC for Her Biden Brain-Freeze for “20 Seconds” on World Stage

One unnamed Democratic strategist who advised statewide candidates in the midterms put the problem in the simplest of terms.

Said the consultant, “Everyone’s waiting on Kamala and AOC. They’ll be building [their campaigns] around the two of them.”

news.title: Crypto CEOs Who Spent the Last Few Years Bootlicking Trump Are Now Stumbling Over Themselves to Proclaim Their Allegiance to the Democratic Party
news.text:
The grifters and hucksters emboldened by Donald Trump are now tripping over themselves to curry favor with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress. Chief among them are the titans of the crypto industry, whose businesses have achieved something akin to institutional legitimacy under the last few years of Republican rule.

But things are looking tense for the blockchain crowd now, after industry spending groups burned some $200 million backing Republican candidates in the US midterms in efforts that decidedly failed to pay off.

In particular, crypto lobbyists went all-out to defeat now-incoming Ohio Senator Sherrod Brown, spending over $55 million on his race alone. It’s now Brown’s second stare-down with the blockchain barons, and according to reporting by Politico, many Democrats aren’t in a forgiving mood.

As pro-crypto Democratic senator Ruben Gallego put it: “they’re f**ked.”

The tone from crypto trade groups is now meeker than arguably ever before. CEO of the crypto firm Digital Chamber Cody Carbone told Politico that the industry needs to pivot from antagonizing Democrats to embracing “an education-first mindset.”

Carbone added that the midterm elections were a “wake-up call” for crypto lobbyists and the companies they champion, and that the industry needs to “lean into both sides equally.”

And as Sheila Warren, the former CEO of an industry firm called the Crypto Council for Innovation told Politico, the lobby’s financial war on Democrats like Ohio’s SHerrod Brown was “boneheaded.”

“So it looks like just a show of force,” Warren explained, “and that’s never a good look, especially when you lose.”

All that said, the degree to which Democratic leadership will seek to antagonize the crypto lobby in 2027 is still up in the air. The last days of the Biden administration were marked by Democratic moves to cozy up to the industry, with a coalition forming to urge then-Vice President Kamala Harris to adopt a more pro-crypto stance. 

For her part, Harris seemed to have acquiesced. During her ill-fated presidential run in 2024, she announced a bizarre policy move to push crypto on Black men — an initiative largely viewed as the Democratic establishment’s capitulation in the face of massive industry spending on Harris’s campaign.

news.title: Buoyed by midterms, Democrats start looking to 2028
news.text: Since Democrats' landslide victories in this month's midterm elections, the party has been consumed by a near-term task — how to quickly deliver promised relief to Americans when the new Congress convenes in January. Alongside that effort is the longer-term conversation about how to capture the White House in 2028 and who will vie to carry the party's mantle. Top Democrats have yet to announce candidacies, and the party is still basking in its historic victories. Nevertheless, the two weeks following the midterms have seen a flurry of activity, including a conference in Denver where more than a dozen influential Democrats laid out ideas for the party's future. "Democrats across the country feel really good. That has prompted a lot of conversations about where to go from here and what does 2028 look like," said Joe Caiazzo, a Democratic strategist who worked on the presidential campaigns of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). On Thursday, allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris launched a draft committee urging her to run. Such committees have also sprung up postelection for Silicon Valley Rep. Ro Khanna, New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. "There's mass amounts of energy," Matthew Taylor, who is heading the Harris-aligned draft committee, said of the general party mood. "Democrats have big, bold plans on what we want to accomplish, and we can't accomplish that without 2028 — and the process does start now." Sen. Alex Padilla of California, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Buttigieg have announced forthcoming books. And various figures have planned travel stops, including New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, who was in South Carolina on Friday, and Harris, who was reported to have a Friday meeting in Paris with French President Emmanuel Macron. California Gov. Gavin Newsom likewise has continued efforts to cast himself as an alternative to President Trump on the world and domestic stages, making a surprise trip to Ukraine after attending the United Nations conference on climate change in Turkey. Newsom then headed to Capitol Hill, where on Wednesday he unveiled an AI framework, addressed national anxiety following tech outages and made jabs at the "lack of leadership" in Washington under Trump. The 2028 presidential election will be a race to chart America's course after a decade that has been dominated by Trump, and it will be the first presidential race in which both parties have wide-open primaries since 2016. For Democrats, the chance to wrest back control of the White House after their bruising 2024 loss carries stakes many view as existential. "They are absolutely determined to win, because most Democrats feel that Trump has done worse harm to this country than any president in anybody's memory," said Elaine Kamarck, director of the Brookings Institution's Center for Effective Public Management and the author of a book on primary politics. "They're absolutely ready to win, and I think you saw that in the way people ran their 2026 races." Throughout the midterm campaign season, likely contenders traveled the country to meet voters and stump for Democratic candidates, helping boost their own visibility in key swing states while working as party surrogates. Now, potential contenders have a window of time before declaring their candidacies to hire staff, talk to party leaders in various states — chatter has already emerged about which hopefuls made calls to new Democratic stars after the midterms — and court fundraisers and donors. "It does feel like the shadow primary is underway," said Jim Demers, a veteran Democratic strategist in New Hampshire, traditionally a testing ground for presidential hopefuls. "I would expect that after the first of the year, we will see the pace pick up, sort of like shifting into the next gear." The Democratic field is expected to be large; jokes about whether all the contenders will fit on the debate stage abound. While the supporters behind draft committees are lining up for their picks, many party activists and donors are interested in a robust primary. "Talking to a lot of our activists here, people are not ready to make any early commitments," Demers said. "They are very much wanting to see the field, hear them and then make their decision." In a poll released this month pitting various Democrats against Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who are widely seen as possible Republican front-runners, the Democratic candidate was favored over Vance or Rubio by voters surveyed in seven swing states. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff led the pack, up 9 points over the Republicans, on average. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear followed, all favored by 7 points, according to the survey, conducted by Impact Research with Equis Research and HIT Strategies. Of California's possible contenders, surveyed voters favored Khanna over Vance or Rubio by 3 percentage points on average, Newsom by 2 points and Harris by 1. Ocasio-Cortez was the only Democrat named in the survey who tied on average with Vance or Rubio rather than outperforming them. Another poll from Reuters/Ipsos showed Ossoff, Buttigieg, Vance and Rubio as the top 2028 contenders. Of Republican voters polled, 45% said Rubio would be an excellent candidate and 43% said Vance would; of Democratic voters polled, 29% each said the same of Buttigieg and Ossoff. The Republican conversation has largely centered on Vance and Rubio, though figures outside the Trump administration such as Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz are also viewed as positioned for possible runs. How the party advances without Trump at the top of the ticket, and whether voters choose to follow the MAGA path or deviate, will be key questions in the GOP primary. In the days since the midterms, leaders across the Democratic political spectrum have agreed — and warned — that the party must deliver results in the next Congress in order to retain the swing voters who gave them the blue wave. The party will need to succeed at "getting something done" in Washington in order to win loyalty from voters who backed blue candidates in this month's elections out of dissatisfaction with the GOP rather than out of affinity for Democrats, said Luke Nichter, chair of presidential studies at Chapman University. "The strategy there is to convert voters who were voting against something," Nichter said, "who maybe in 2028 can vote for something."

news.title: Barabak: A blue Texas is a monumental shift. That's already reshaping the 2028 presidential race
news.text: In 2020, when Joe Biden came within 5 percentage points of winning Texas, it was cause for Democratic celebration. Biden, en route to the White House, turned in the strongest performance by a Democratic presidential candidate in a quarter-century, More promising, it seemed as though he'd built on Hillary Clinton's showing in 2016, when she lost the state by 9 points. Visions of a blue Texas danced before eager Democratic eyes. Then came 2024. Donald Trump clobbered Kamala Harris by double digits. Texas — fast-growing, demographically changing — had long stymied Democrats, who believed the booming Latino population, in particular, guaranteed success. The state was a chimera, a blue mirage, a plum that always lay beyond the party's plucking. Until Nov. 3. In one of the most stunning outcomes in a midterm election filled with jaw-dropping surprises, Democrats captured each and every one of the top statewide offices in Texas, claimed a U.S. Senate seat, flipped the House of Representatives and defeated all four Republicans seeking reelection to the state Supreme Court. This after failing to win a single statewide office in more than 30 years. But the GOP drubbing is not just something for Democrats to crow about. The red-to-blue transformation represents a monumental shift that carries nationwide implications, not least in reshaping the 2028 presidential race. "There's a lot of levels," said Mike Madrid, a Republican strategist and expert on the Latino vote. "There's the narrative. There's morale. There's demographics. There's the road map to 270," the number of electoral votes it takes to win the White House. Only a fool would venture to say how Texas — which hasn't gone Democratic in a presidential election since 1976 — will vote two years from now. (Don't look at me like that.) Especially based on the outcome of a single, extraordinary election. Much will depend on the presidential nominees, how much they raise and where, when the screws tighten, the candidates and their allies choose to allocate their time and money. But the plain fact is Republicans can no longer assume Texas is all locked up, as they have for well over a generation. To do so would be suicidal, said Dave Carney, a campaign strategist for the state's last two governors, Rick Perry and Greg Abbott. The GOP, Carney said, is "going to have to have a command focus" to win back the state in 2028. That alone is a huge development and, potentially, the most significant change to the presidential map since 1992, when another reliably Republican state turned blue — for the next 30 years it turned out, and counting. When Bill Clinton won California in 1992, he became the first Democrat to do so since Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964. It wasn't a particularly impressive victory. Clinton carried the state with just 46% of the vote in a three-way contest with President George H.W. Bush and independent Ross Perot. Many, including Clinton and those around him, feared the showing might be a one-off, with California reverting to Republican form at the first opportunity. So Clinton devoted the next four years to solidifying his support, lavishing money and endless attention on California, which helped turn the state into the blue bastion we know today. In 1996, Clinton crushed Republican Bob Dole by 13 percentage points. No Republican has come close to winning the state since; few presidential candidates have even tried to compete. That effective GOP surrender was hugely consequential. It freed Democrats to spend hundreds of millions of dollars elsewhere, including the battlegrounds of the Midwest and states such as Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, North Carolina and Virginia. which once seemed beyond reach. Now the opposite is true. Money and resources that Republicans might have devoted to other states may need to be invested in Texas, an enormously expensive state which, for decades, has been foundational to the GOP's presidential success. The state's 40 electoral votes are second only to California, which has 54. It's hard to see how Republicans make up that deficit if they fail to carry Texas. There's been a self-defeating, self-perpetuating cycle that vexed Democrats for years. Winning Texas seemed like an extreme long shot at the presidential level, so the party and its candidates refused to invest the considerable sum needed to make the state competitive. Because they declined to make that investment, the state never grew truly competitive. With Democrats in control in Austin and the state's incoming governor, Gina Hinojosa, and U.S. senator, James Talarico, positioned to bulk up the party's fundraising and organizational muscle, those days are over. It's not, however, as if Texas suddenly leans Democratic. Hinojosa and Talarico are both relative moderates, especially compared with most blue-state Democrats, which explains at least some of their success. "Do I think [California Gov.] Gavin Newsom has a chance of carrying Texas? No," said Karl Rove, who worked to turn the state into a Republican fortress before helping put Gov. George W. Bush to the White House. "Do I think [Illinois Gov.] JB Pritzker has a chance? No. Do I think someone who's a centrist could? It depends who the Republican is. "The further left the candidate, the less likely it is they're going to be competitive in this state," Rove said. "The larger their wallet, the more likely it is they can afford to come in and play." John Anzalone, a Democratic pollster who has worked in several presidential campaigns, including Biden's 2020 run, agreed it's far too soon to size up the 2028 landscape. What is clear, Anzalone said, is that after statewide wins in places such as Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi "the electoral battleground map has expanded" and Democrats "will be spending in states [where] we haven't spent in a long time." Also clear: Texas is no longer a certain Democratic heartbreaker, beckoning but invariably falling outside their reach.
news.summary: It's been 50 years since a Democrat won the state, but after a midterm blowout Texas is now competitive. The shift is the most significant change to the presidential map since California went blue.
news.author: Mark Z. Barabak

news.title: Why the U.S. midterms might have ended JD Vance's presidential hopes
news.text:
JD Vance's presidential ambitions for 2028 could be among the most significant political casualties of the Democratic blue wave in this month's U.S. midterm elections.

His chances of becoming the Republican candidate in two years may have suffered a more recent blow, as reports suggest U.S. President Donald Trump has begun to sour on his vice-president.

"Despite years of work to keep his feet glued to Trump’s MAGA coattails, [Vance] is probably losing any semblance of hope that he’ll get to be a GOP frontrunner in 2028," New York Intelligencer staff editor Chas Danner wrote in an article under the headline "JD Vance’s presidential dream is being snuffed out."

"At the beginning of the year, Vance was widely seen as the GOP’s presumptive 2028 nominee. He may end the year as the presumptive also-ran, if that."

Over at the conservative magazine National Review, senior writer Noah Rothman also weighed in on what he views as Vance's diminishing political fortunes, saying, "Those who invested in JD Vance’s political stock ... may be looking to offload their holdings."

AnalysisJD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

Vance hasn’t publicly said if he will run for president in 2028, but before the midterms, he was considered a front-runner, with perhaps the highest name recognition of any potential candidate. 

However, since the midterms, Vance's aspirations "have suffered, because he's Donald Trump's vice-president," said Michael Traugott, a research professor emeritus at the University of Michigan's Center for Political Studies, in an interview with CBC News.

Exit polls suggested Republicans lost the election over issues relating to inflation and the cost of living, government corruption and the war in Iran.

"The problem is that the vice-president can't separate himself very easily from the administration's policies," Traugott said.

Donors express concerns about Vance

According to the Wall Street Journal, after the Democrats' success in taking the House of Representatives and Senate in the midterms, some Republican donors began making calls to senior party members and expressing concerns that they couldn't back Vance, because he's too tied to an unpopular administration.

This illustrates the challenge Vance faces: Do Republican primary voters want a candidate who has broader support among the general public but isn't directly connected to the president, or will they only support someone who has Trump's endorsement?

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist, told Reuters.

Trump hasn’t endorsed Vance or anyone else. Reports have also emerged recently that Vance himself is not so sure about a run, particularly in the wake of the Republicans' disastrous showing in the midterms.

In Republican primaries, Trump still commands a lot of votes and a lot of respect, Martin Cohen, a political science professor with James Madison University, told CBC News.

"I would definitely think that the front-runner would be the candidate with Trump's endorsement, if he does give one," he said.

Vance blamed Iran war for midterm losses

That means Vance will have to get his boss's approval, as well as the support of the MAGA base, while "trying to distance himself a little bit, at least," Cohen said.

Vance's attempt to distance himself from the administration may have already begun, with possible consequences. Following the midterms, Vance, in a lengthy post on X, levelled much of the blame for Republican losses on the war in Iran.

"If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance wrote. "Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest."

Vance, who according to reports has for a while privately expressed reservations about the war, has simultaneously argued that there's "no daylight" between him and the president on Iran. 

In response to the X post, Trump agreed Iran may have been a factor in the midterm losses. But he also insisted that invading Iran was the right policy decision.

Trump told reporters that Vance's post should have added, "'If you had it to do again, would you do it again?' The answer is yes."

Soon after the X post, the vice-president, who had been leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, was taken off the file. 

Posting on Truth Social, Trump said his administration no longer needed a deal with Iran and that he wanted Vance to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states.

Why the war in Iran might cost Trump and the Republicans at the ballot boxWhat the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

Abe Greenwald, the executive editor of Commentary magazine, called Trump's sidelining of Vance a "remarkably skillful work of public humiliation."

Karen Beckwith, a political science professor with Ohio-based Case Western Reserve University, said in an email to CBC News that Trump's removal of Vance from any responsibility for negotiating or interacting with Iranian counterparts "undermines Vance as a potential presidential nominee in 2028."

Meanwhile, Fox News host Brian Kilmeade lashed out at Vance after his interview with Kilmeade's colleague Laura Ingraham, in which Vance said there were some who want the Iran war to go on indefinitely.

Kilmeade rejected that assertion, calling it "another straw man" argument from Vance, while adding that "he never should have been vice-president."

Trump reportedly frustrated with Vance

Beckwith said this could leave Vance without any substantive achievements on which to campaign for the 2028 nomination — unlike potential opponents like Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Republican governors and senators.

Asked about his social media post about Iran at a news conference on Friday, Vance, flanked by both Trump and Rubio, said the president makes the decision, that the president has said he would attack Iran again and that it's his job to support the president.

Vance's comments followed a New York Times report earlier this week that Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how Vance has framed his assessment of what went wrong in Iran, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran.

According to the Times, Trump has instead been praising Rubio, a strong supporter of the U.S. war against Iran, as a potential presidential candidate.

While past polls have shown Vance as the leading Republican candidate for 2028, a recent poll from Emerson College had Rubio as the top choice.

Presidents in recent history, dating back to Ronald Reagan, have all publicly endorsed their vice-presidents who sought to be their party's candidate for the presidency. That includes Joe Biden's endorsement of Kamala Harris in 2024, despite Biden having been pressured by members of his own party to not run for second term.

"I don't think that Donald Trump is going to be shy about endorsing somebody," Traugott said. "Ordinarily, we would think the vice-president would have an advantage ... so the fact that he may be souring on this relationship is very important. Even if they were to say that [Trump] was remaining neutral, that would be a slap in the face of that."

Yet some political observers are cautious about writing Vance's political obituary just yet. Republican strategist Mark Bednar told CBC News that Vance has developed good connections to a large donor base within the Republican party over the past couple years.

Iranian officials welcome U.S. midterm results after voters rebuke Trump administration, Iran war

Meanwhile, Republican strategist Barrett Marson told CBC News that Trump may have actually done Vance a favour by taking him off the Iran file. 

"That is an absolute blessing. The less one has to do with this immensely unpopular war, the better you are off politically."

Marson added that there's still a lot of time before 2028, meaning things could improve to Vance's benefit. For example, gas prices could come down significantly, interest rates for homes could drop and voters could start to view the economy in positive terms.

"Two years is just an eternity," Marson said. "Especially in Donald Trump's America."
news.author: Mark Gollom
