news.title: PBS Tosses Softballs at Gov. Shapiro, No Zinger on Internal Democrat Battle on Israel
news.text:
The PBS News Hour loves interviewing Democrats. We found earlier this year that they are more than five times as likely to interview a liberal rather than a conservative. On Friday, PBS anchor Amna Nawaz brought on Gov. Josh Shapiro (D-Penn.) to kick off speculation about whether Shapiro is running for president in 2028.

The first softball in the 11-minute interview was this one: "So I got to ask you, what's the governor of Pennsylvania doing delivering a speech on foreign policy if he's not running for president?"

Then on Iran, it’s that type of question that Democrats get, as in “explain what you would do.”

news.text:
With the midterm blowout in the rearview, the Republican Party has no choice but to shift its focus to 2028. John Doyle, host of BlazeTV’s “The John Doyle Show,” believes Vice President JD Vance is poised to secure the nomination but that success will largely depend on his ability to thread the needle by distancing himself from the administration’s less popular moves while still embracing MAGA.

“By all appearances, as we’ve said, as we’ve been enthused about, JD Vance is probably in the best position to succeed Trump,” he says, citing Race to the White House’s poll aggregator, which names Vance as the top choice for Republicans.

Doyle adds that Trump’s choice of Vance as his running mate makes him the likely front-runner for the president’s endorsement and that as the RNC’s finance chair, Vance has “been able to fundraise for a 2028 presidential bid since March of 2025.”

But even if the tea leaves are right and Vance sails through the primary, there’s still an “uphill battle” awaiting him, he warns.

“JD Vance also has a bit of a problem, and that's the same problem that really any Republican serving in Trump 47 is going to face, and that is the perceived baggage of the administration,” Doyle explains.

“Trump has done a lot of great work, the best work that we've ever seen in terms of the big-picture civilizational issues, but unfortunately, the people are not so focused on that. The people are focused on affordability and gas prices,” he adds.

If he becomes the 2028 nominee, Vance, he argues, will have to “walk this tightrope where you're embracing certain parts of MAGA while distancing yourself from the bad parts that the wider population isn't so hot about.”

“That's not going to be easy to do,” Doyle says. “After all, if he attempts to distance himself too much from certain aspects of Trump 47, he risks the problem that sometimes Donald Trump doesn't like that, right? He might get some Truth Social posts about him.”

But that’s not Vance’s only issue, he says.

“A bigger problem, though, is maybe voters will wonder, wait a minute, you were in office — why didn't you do things differently? This is the same problem that Kamala Harris encountered in 2024, right?” Doyle says.

“It's like it was obvious the Biden administration had failed in so many ways. Naturally, Kamala Harris had to try to kind of like distance herself from that, but as we saw, it didn't work. Voters associated her correctly with this disastrous Brandon administration. That's the position Vance finds himself in,” he continues.

Doyle clarifies that he’s not “comparing the disastrous nature of the Brandon admin to the Trump admin” but rather making the point that “it is very difficult to distance yourself from an administration in which you were the second in command.”

The good news is that Vance still has two years to put himself in the best position to run in 2028.

“If Vance wants to win, he's going to have to be the face of the administration's efforts to lower costs, which to his credit, he, more than anyone, I think, has spoken about this coherently. He's made a real effort to sell this to the American public,” Doyle argues, floating the idea of Vance heading “some kind of affordability task force … to show Americans that the administration is understanding their concerns.”

“Vance is talented in a lot of ways,” he continues. “I would put him up against anybody in just raw ability to do the campaign, do the debates, all of that, but still, to be a Republican in 2028 and to win is an uphill battle.”

news.title: Dems Grapple With A Wide-Open Presidential Race — And No Clear Front-Runner
news.text:
Welcome to the most wide-open Democratic presidential primary in two decades.

Party operatives looking at the potential field of candidates (and often trying to get a job with said candidates) do not see a juggernaut waiting to bully the rest of the field. Instead, they see a “Big Five”: Former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. 

But of those five, it’s unclear if three of them — Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and Ossoff — will end up running at all.

The result is a (very) early race with absolutely no clear frontrunner, a far cry from former President Joe Biden’s pole position in 2020 or former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton’s clear early dominance in both 2008 and 2016. 

“There’s no clear frontrunner, and even high name ID isn’t necessarily going to translate to success,” said Josh Schwerin, a Democratic strategist with extensive presidential campaign experience, adding: “The eventual nominee is going to have to salvage the terrible reputation of the Democratic Party, and the primary is shaping up to be a very healthy debate about who is the best leader for that challenge.”

Most close observers of the race do not expect candidates to start entering the race in earnest until March. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is widely expected to be the first person to enter the contest, though he has said he won’t make a final decision until after the holidays. At a recent Democratic-run gathering in Denver, most of the rumored potential candidates seemed to kick the tires, sheepishly declaring that they should be the chosen leader.

And of the five leading contenders, it’s unclear whether a majority even want the job. 

Ossoff has publicly ruled out the prospect and committed to serving his full six-year term, citing his desire to spend time with his young family. Ocasio-Cortez has a choice between running for president or running for the U.S. Senate seat held by incoming Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, with many Democrats in New York expecting she’ll prefer the latter. And Harris ― who leads most early primary polls ― has not publicly indicated an announcement timeline, though nearly a dozen of her former aides are now on her payroll, according to independent reporter Zohreen Shah.

Earlier this week, former second gentleman Douglas Emoff said Harris is currently reflecting and will share more in her own time.

“She was really heartened to listen, to hear what people had to say, to support different types of candidates up and down the ticket, not just at the national level, but at the state and local level,” Emhoff said at an event in Los Angeles. “All these offices matter. And that’s what she spent her time doing. And now she’s going to reflect and make a decision, and you’ll all hear it when you hear it.”

The other two leading candidates, Newsom and Buttigieg, are seen as near-certain to run. Buttigieg announced earlier this week he will release a book in January. Newsom has said he won’t run if Harris does — which most Democrats have interpreted as an implicit prediction that Harris will not. Both are seen as flawed leaders, with questions about Buttigieg’s ability to appeal to Black and Latino voters and murmurs that Newsom’s stock peaked a year ago.

A second tier of candidates is moving more aggressively towards a bid. A top aide to Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) recently left Giffords — the gun control group named after his wife — to advise him directly again, while Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro gave a foreign policy-focused speech in Philadelphia on Friday. 

But right now the most active efforts are coming from draft groups not directly affiliated with the candidates they support. 

At least half a dozen groups (and growing) aimed at drafting their favorite Democrat to run have popped up over the last few weeks, including one for Harris. These draft organizations for Harris, Ocasio-Cortez, Buttigieg, Ossoff, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Khanna and former Rep. Rahm Emanuel (Ill.) are gathering names and emails that have the potential to spawn more robust organizing and volunteer infrastructures for their preferred candidate if they decide to jumpstart a bid. 

And they are full steam ahead, with or without buy-in from their principal. 

Some groups, like “Team Pete PAC” are encouraging supporters to engage potential voters with host house parties and fundraisers, with an emphasis on community service, said Jennifer Holdsworth, the former campaign manager of Buttigieg’s DNC chair run, who will help lead the PAC alongside other allies of the former South Bend, Indiana, mayor.

And despite what’s bound to be an elbows-out primary, they’re not hoarding their resources — if Buttigieg isn’t the nominee, their group is happy to share them with whoever the nominee ends up being, Holdsworth said. She believes that most other Democrats are more prone to support over sniping these days anyhow. 

“I think that the field is going to be extraordinarily exciting. I’ve been in and around Democratic politics for around 25 years, and I’ve not yet seen the type of excitement at the beginning of the process this much,” Holdsworth told HuffPost. “I’m really hearing people talk about how excited they are right at the beginning, and I’m not hearing in real life a lot of sniping against any of the candidates. I think everybody is just completely moved that there’s so many people that may or may not be interested in it.”

“Ready for AOC” is also building a list of potential volunteers.

“Winning won’t be easy, but it will be worth it,” the group says. “AOC won’t have the backing of billionaire donors eager to line the pockets of candidates they know they can control. If we want AOC to win in 2028, the work starts now, and it starts with us.”

The “Run Kamala Run PAC” will host its first virtual kickoff event this Saturday, headlined by Chris Walton, former Chair of the Democratic Party of Milwaukee County, Wisconsin. The group is touting Harris as a frontrunner despite media skepticism.

“The media narrative is wrong. People like Kamala Harris, and they want her to run again,” said Matthew Taylor, president and treasurer of Run Kamala Run PAC, in a statement announcing the event. “More than 6,000 people signed up before we were even a PAC. Now we’re making it official.”

news.title: White women just broke with the GOP. Can Democrats keep them?
news.text:
White women didn’t break for Democrats in 2016, when Hillary Clinton ran as the first woman nominated for president by a major party. They didn’t break for Democrats two years later, when a blue wave swept the House. They didn’t break after Donald Trump’s Supreme Court picks helped overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. And they didn’t break when Kamala Harris faced Trump in 2024.

This month, they did.

For the first time since 1992, a majority of white women, the country’s largest demographic voting bloc, voted for House Democrats, according to The Voter Poll. It was a blow to a coalition that powered all three of Trump’s White House bids.

Analysts say it’s clear why 53% of those women backed Democrats this year.

“White women were driven very early on by the cost-corruption agenda,” Celinda Lake, a veteran Democratic pollster, told MS NOW. She was referring to the party’s focus on affordability and corruption in the Trump administration.

“They really felt the affordability agenda — even before gas prices took off,” Lake said. “They felt food, healthcare and utilities getting more expensive.”

Like every other demographic group, white women told The Voter Poll that the economy was the most important issue facing the country. The state of democracy was a close second for them; no other subgroup ranked that issue as highly. More than 90% of white women said both the cost of living and corruption were crucial or major factors in their vote for Congress. That put them on par with Latino men and a few points ahead of white men. (Larger shares of Black men, Black women and Latinas said the same.)

Amanda Iovino, a Republican pollster who worked with Lake in the past, agreed that Democrats did a better job of tying policies coming out of Washington to rising costs at home.

“I think we took our finger off the pulse of ‘how do we talk to women and what are women saying,’ and I think it’s a matter of listening to those voters again,” she said.

Democrats don’t need a majority of white women to win. Black women, Asian American women and Latinas have long been strong supporters of the party. White women, by contrast, backed Republicans in all but two presidential elections in the second half of the 20th century. But if enough white women stay with the party, they and the women of color who have long been its backbone “can keep the Democrats in office for a decade or more,” Lake said.

The question now is whether Democrats can hold on to them.

“I've been saying that we flipped a whole lot of seats this election. Now we want to see our leaders flip some tables,” said Katie Paris, founder and CEO of Red, Wine & Blue, a progressive advocacy group that mobilizes women in suburban swing districts. “People are serious about wanting to see a change.”

‘Race, religion and marriage’ kept white women with the GOP

This year’s shift has roots in Trump’s first term.

In 2016 more than half of white women voted for Trump, according to exit polls. Two years later, some had soured on his party: In the 2018 midterms, white women split evenly at 49% in House races. That election came a month after the contentious confirmation of Justice Brett Kavanaugh, Trump’s second Supreme Court nominee. At the time, “white college-educated women were getting really nervous about having the right to abortion taken away, which they never thought was possible,” Lake said.

But by 2020, they were back: 55% backed Trump in his loss to Joe Biden.

In June 2022, Kavanaugh and Trump’s two other appointees, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett, joined the majority in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, which overturned the constitutional right to abortion. But even that didn’t shake white women, 53% of whom voted for Trump in 2024.

That loyalty reflects the group’s broader allegiance to the GOP. Lake said it rests on “race, religion and marriage” to white men, who are among Republicans’ most devoted voting blocs.

White women “benefit from their association with white men, who are at the top of the social hierarchy,” said Tiffany Barnes, a professor of government at the University of Texas at Austin who co-authored a 2018 paper on white women’s support for Republicans in the 2012 and 2016 elections. That’s especially true, she added, for “women who otherwise feel disadvantaged in society,” such as white women without college degrees — 56% of whom backed Republicans this year.

Women dressed as suffragettes cast their ballots at the Polk County Election Office on Oct. 8, 2018, in Des Moines, Iowa.

Still, Democrats gained ground with those voters, winning 42% of them, up from the 35% who backed Harris in 2024. Barnes said the shift reflects an economy in which “women without a college education are going to be hit harder on average than women who maybe have a higher earning capacity.”

College-educated and younger white women drove most of the swing. More than 60% of each group backed Democrats this year, The Voter Poll shows. In 2024, 58% of white college-educated women and 50% of white women under 45 voted for Harris, according to exit polls.

Lake said Democrats now need to do three things: keep the college-educated and younger white women they won by large margins; keep “closing the margin” with white women without degrees; and hold on to women of color.

But analysts warned that turning away from Trump’s GOP is not the same as embracing the Democratic Party. If Democrats don’t deliver, they said, the party could lose these gains quickly.

“People did not rush to the polls to vote for the blue team,” said Paris. “They rushed to the polls to reject the chaos, the corruption and the cruelty of the Trump administration, and they have given Democrats a chance.”

The Voter Poll bears that out. Slightly more of the white women who voted in the midterms said they were Republicans in ideology (37%) than Democrats (35%). More than a quarter called themselves independent or something else.

As Lake said of Democrats: “They’ve got work to do.”

The path forward

There are several key issues where Democrats have the advantage — and where analysts say the party should lean in.

Almost half of white women said Democrats are better able to handle healthcare, a 16-point advantage over Republicans, The Voter Poll found. White women also trust Democrats more on policies affecting transgender people, by 12 points, and on foreign policy, the economy and government corruption, by 4 to 5 points. Two-thirds believe abortion should be legal in all or most cases, in line with the Democratic position.

Immigration is the only issue on which these voters trust Republicans more, but only by 1 point. At the same time, 61% of white women said they disapprove of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is doing its job.

“They think ICE is rogue, criminal and went too far,” Lake said, citing high-profile reports of ICE detaining children and killing U.S. citizens.

White women also rallied against data centers. Eighty-two percent said they would oppose a data center being built in their community. Only Black women opposed them more, at 84%.

Paris saw this firsthand. She said at least three dozen of the events her group held nationwide, attended mostly by white women, focused on the threats posed by data centers.

“Women saw this as a threat to their communities,” she said. “They saw it driving up the cost of energy bills. They saw it going against the will of communities. They saw it as a threat to their children's health.”

Demonstrators protest against "The Barn" data center, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, on July 30, 2026, in Saline, Mich.

Democrats say focusing on the issues on which they hold the advantage is the key to keeping these voters.

The Democratic Women’s Caucus “is ready to deliver for women and families next Congress by lowering costs, repealing Trump’s healthcare cuts, expanding access to affordable childcare and passing paid family leave,” Rep. Deborah Ross, D-N.C., co-chair of the caucus’s Policy Task Force, said in a statement to MS NOW.

In an interview, Libby Schneider, deputy executive director of the Democratic National Committee, pointed to the party’s “progress” with white women without college degrees. She also acknowledged that it has more work to do.

“We have to be a party that understands what folks who are working every day are going through,” she said.

Schneider said the national party would keep paying for state parties to hire organizers, open field offices and register voters, as it did before the midterms.

“Rather than starting from scratch a few months before an election, that year-round on-the-ground engagement with voters helped Democrats make important gains and win white women for the first time in decades,” she said.

A DNC spokesperson declined to share data on how many white women the party registered ahead of the midterms.

Republicans agree less on how to win back one of their most loyal voting blocs.

Tina Descovich is co-founder and CEO of Moms for Liberty, the conservative group that has rallied people across the country to run for school boards and has backed restrictions on children’s books in libraries. She told MS NOW that Republicans should double down on education and parental rights to win back the voters they lost. She noted that ballot measures restricting transgender kids from playing on girls’ sports teams passed in all four states that voted on them, including the blue states of Washington and Colorado.

“Our issues are winning issues,” Descovich said, though she added that they also did not “rise to the top of the issues that people were concerned about” in this election.

Iovino said those issues “do matter to a segment of voters.” But she said the most important things for the party’s future were building a new bench of “really good quality candidates, particularly women candidates” (whom Republicans have long struggled to recruit), and listening to voters’ top priorities.

Asked about the GOP’s loss of white women, Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement: “Democrats aren’t even in power yet and they’re foaming at the mouth to impeach Republicans and raise taxes — neither of which address affordability. Meanwhile, Republicans remain focused on ending insider trading, putting more money in working families’ pockets, and putting America first to win back control in 2028.”

It’s not yet clear whether a post-Trump GOP can win white women back. If they can’t, Lake said, the party will have the president to blame.

“Trump was holding those women for a long time,” Lake said, “and he just kept making their lives harder and harder.”

news.title: America elects record 5 Black governors. How did they make history?
news.text:
Before he earned five degrees, Nevada Gov.-elect Aaron Ford became a single dad during his junior year at Texas A&M University in the early 1990s.

Now Ford is breaking the typical mold of past governors in another way, as one of five incoming Black governors elected on Nov. 3.

Ford, 54, will join a historic number of elected Black governors alongside Florida Gov.-elect Bryon Donalds, a Republican, and three fellow Democrats: incumbent Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, Wisconsin's David Crowley and Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia, who will be the nation's first Black woman governor.

More: Black victories, Red States: Scott Colom and the new era of Black leaders

Many of the candidates centered their winning campaigns on affordability and used their personal experiences with financial hardship and poverty to help relate with voters.

Ford, the Nevada attorney general, turned to a conversation with a voter on the campaign trail in North Las Vegas as he addressed his achievement and the historic milestone for Black political power during a phone interview.

"He told me his story and, you know, how he was struggling with affordability issues and I said to him, 'I didn't run to make history. I ran because of his story,'" Ford told USA TODAY. "His story being one where times are tough for him right now."

Meet the record 5 Black governors elected to lead states

George Washington University professor Jasmine Carrera Smith said Black politicians often deemphasize race when trying to win elections and again when addressing the historic nature of their victories.

The United States is 13.5% Black, according to U.S. Census data. No U.S. state has a majority-Black population and there have only been three elected Black governors in U.S. history, all Democrats. Moore, who was first elected Maryland governor in 2022, is the only Black governor currently.

The nation's first Black elected governor, Virginia's Douglas Wilder, was elected in 1989, and Deval Patrick was elected governor of Massachusetts in 2006. Then-Lt. Gov. David Paterson became New York's first Black governor in 2008 when Gov. Eliot Spitzer resigned. Paterson completed his term but did not run for election in 2010.

A record nine Black nominees

This cycle was expected to be historic for Black gubernatorial candidates – a quarter, or nine, of the 36 contests featured Black major-party nominees.

The field of nine nominees were sprawled across red, blue and purple states.

Races in Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, South Carolina and Wisconsin all featured Black nominees.

From the outset, Moore in heavily Democratic Maryland and Donalds, a conservative who represents a coastal South Florida congressional district, were most likely to win their respective races. There were three Republicans − Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth and Michigan U.S. Rep John James − while the remaining six were Democrats.

Donalds, an ally to President Donald Trump, faced an onslaught of racial attacks from a primary opponent, James Fishback, who said the three-term congressman was a "slave" to billionaire donors.

Ford, the first Black official elected statewide in Nevada history in 2018, unseated Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in the battleground state.

In Georgia, Bottoms, who led Atlanta as mayor during the COVID-19 pandemic, was the second Black woman nominated for governor after former Georgia state Rep. Stacey Abrams, the Democratic candidate in unsuccessful races against Gov. Brian Kemp in 2018 and 2022. Bottoms defeated Rick Jackson, a billionaire who financed his own campaign.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley won a competitive primary to face right-wing House Freedom Caucus member, Rep. Tom Tiffany. Crowley grew up in Milwaukee, one of America's most segregated cities, according to data from the Othering and Belonging Institute at UC Berkeley.

Moore, the nation's third Black elected governor, made it a personal mission to see more Black governors in office and campaigned for the trio of newly elected Democrats.

"They know the assignment isn't to make history, it's to make child poverty history, to make low wages history, to make income inequality history," Moore said of Ford, Bottoms and Crowley in a statement shared with USA TODAY on Nov. 16.

More: A record number of Black candidates are running for governor in 2026

'We embrace our diversity'

The Democratic Governors' Association, led by Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, and its allies spent over $70 million to more than double the nation's number of Black governors.

The DGA was Bottoms' biggest financial backer with nearly $20 million spent in the race, while the DGA and its allies, including A More Affordable Nevada, were Ford's largest outside donor with over $26 million spent during the race.

A DGA-aligned group, Protect Our Wisconsin, was also Crowley's biggest outside funder with over $22 million spent to topple Tiffany.

Ford, Bottoms and Crowley will govern three of the seven crucial battleground states in presidential elections, in addition to Arizona, Michigan, North Carolina and Pennsylvania.

"I've always disagreed with folks that think a certain place won't elect a woman or someone from a different background," DGA chair Beshear told USA TODAY. "I think that the United States said very clearly that they were tired of the cruelty and the division and that we embrace our diversity."

How a Nina Simone song resonates in Scott Colom's Mississippi Senate win

Beshear says America embraced diversity

After former Vice President Kamala Harris lost to Trump in 2024, some Democrats suggested that the party run a White male nominee (and Christian, as a March report in Axios said) which would eliminate many of the potential 2028 contenders.

The respective wins by the group of governors-elect upended ideas about who is electable, according to political experts.

Paru Shah, a political scientist at Rutgers University, previously told USA TODAY before Election Day that outcomes at the polls are more dependent on partisanship and the political environment than personal identity.

Democrats swept races across the country, even in unfriendlier territory, in the Nov. 3 blue wave.

"The broader idea is that, you know, when candidates of color, women of color run and are supported, they can win and maybe even do even better than, you know, White candidates or the men candidates can," according to Bernard Fraga, a political science professor at Emory University.

In Texas, Beshear and the DGA faced criticism from some Latino leaders for the organization's lack of investment in Gov.-elect Gina Hinajosa, who will become the state's first Hispanic governor.

A Politico article Nov. 8 chronicled lingering resentment toward the 2028 hopeful, but Beshear pushed back on the concerns in a phone call Nov. 13.

Wes Moore: I was America's only Black governor. I'm happy to lose that title

"Gina Hinojosa ran away with it, won by seven points. When you compare that to, say, Kansas where we were able to send different types of money, we only won by 7,000 votes," Beshear told USA TODAY. "And so I think we invested where we needed to, how much we needed to, to come out with the maximum number of wins."

The newly elected Black Democrats won by similarly commanding margins. Bottoms beat Jackson by over 8 percentage points. Crowley prevailed over Tiffany by 8 percentage points. And Ford bested Lombardo by more than 7 percentage points.

Donalds won by just over 1% in his race against former Rep. David Jolly.

Donalds told Kristen Welker on "Meet the Press" after the election Nov. 8 that his victory is "really a matter of personal pride" while the collective wins are "a matter of pride for Black Americans all through the country."

Once a single dad in college, Ford is now the married father of three young Black men as well as his nephew, who is raised by the family.

"I've always wanted to be certain that they had a role model in their father who they could emulate and who would demonstrate to them that they can be whatever it is they want to," Ford told USA TODAY.

Ford's oldest son, Avery, whom he had in college, is now in residency after attending medical school at Georgetown. Ford says the father-son duo went from Medicaid to medicine. In January, they will go to the governor's mansion.

news.title: Promise Me, America by Joe Biden review – former president defends his decisions
news.text:
Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party.

Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with Mitt Romney in 2012, when Biden was VP. Caught cold, Obama prepared for the next one and cruised to re-election.

During his own debate, Biden was utterly lost, stuttering out: “We finally beat … Medicare.” He writes now that he meant “big pharma”, but a bad cold got the better of him. It’s just not enough. Biden writes a lot about taking responsibility. But he doesn’t. Prompted by his description of his wife’s support – “Get up. We’re not going to let 90 minutes define your career” – anyone with the stomach might turn to another book out this week, The East Wing by Azadeh Moaveni, for an account of First Lady Jill Biden’s role that dreadful summer, refusing to look fate in the eye. After that, anyone might reach for a very strong drink.

Readers might also choose other books’ proper accounts of other traumas, including Biden’s muddled interview with special counsel Robert Hur, who investigated Biden’s retention of classified information, and the legal travails of Biden’s son Hunter. Biden says Hur’s famous description of “an elderly man with a poor memory” was a political hit job. Hunter got a pardon. So did other family members, for protection against Donald Trump. The pardon power is an absurd anachronism in need of drastic reform. Perhaps we should thank Biden for making that so clear.

It’s less clear what Promise Me, America is really for. Biden’s third book, it is his third with “promise” in the title. Promises to Keep came out in 2007, when Biden was a Delaware senator preparing a second run for president. Promise Me, Dad dealt with the death of his son, Beau, at the end of Biden’s eight years as vice-president to Barack Obama, and laid the ground for his third presidential run.

What does Biden want America to promise him now? Maybe just to pony up 30 bucks one last time. The former president is 84. His cancer diagnosis hangs over his book, discussed with admirable candor.

The book is well written and well organized, if sometimes close to a recitation of Biden’s daybook as he won the White House in 2020, beating Trump; as he governed through four stormy years at home and abroad; as Trump loomed again; as Biden faltered and stumbled and finally stood down in a summer of disaster. Biden, as both a leader and writer, may be no Ulysses S Grant, author of the best presidential memoir. As a writer, or leader, he may be no Obama, a comparison that hangs silently over every part of Promise Me, America. But as a president, Biden did make his mark.

Though memories of his presidency have been swallowed by Trumpian chaos, most know Biden presided over major legislation to help the country (and the world, via vaccine programs) emerge from the ravages of Covid. Chapters about how the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act got through Congress are rich reading as the Trump administration flails and fails amid systems outages and after a midterms beating.

A theory: Promise Me, America is the memoir of a man who became president but whose heart remained in the Senate. Biden was a senator 36 years, elected at 29 in 1972, known as “Amtrak Joe” for his habit of traveling by train from Delaware to DC and back, father to young sons left motherless when his wife, Neilia Biden, and daughter Naomi were killed in a car crash. When Biden became vice-president, he was 66. Steeped in the lore of the Senate, the back-room dealing and backslapping, he may even have managed to read all of Master of the Senate, Robert Caro’s doorstop about Lyndon Johnson, to whom Biden is often compared.

To pass the American Rescue Plan, Joe Manchin, of West Virginia, simply had to be won over. Biden relishes how it was done: “I called Joe [Manchin] to meet with me in the Oval Office… We were both Catholic politicians from the old school. Proud. Stubborn. But now it was time to lay our cards on the table. This was my first major legislative initiative. The American people needed relief. I needed him on this vote. I never considered myself a Lyndon Johnson-type president, who cajoled and threatened and even physically cowed legislators, but I was losing my temper. I told Joe that I needed him on this, and if he screwed me, I’d go to every county in West Virginia and tell them that Joe Manchin was why they weren’t getting any help. Joe came right back at me, reminding me that I wasn’t so popular in West Virginia. After a further exchange of words, Joe agreed to be with me and vote in favor.”

As a “Catholic politician from the old school”, Biden’s faith is never far from the surface. His forgiveness was strained by Manchin, who in December 2021 turned and shivved his president, going on Fox News to declare himself a no on the Build Back Better bill, sinking it. Biden also celebrates William Scranton, a Pennsylvania governor who Biden’s “grandpop” – a typically folksy phrase – held up as a politician who “smacks you on the back, like he’s your best friend … and it’s not until you’re about a block or so from his house that you notice the feeling of warm blood running down your back. That, Joey, is what we call a ‘silk stocking screw’.”

Alas, as the Manchin episode shows, Biden is a backslapper but, fatal for any politician, a nice guy, no sort of killer at all. Tales of stern statesmanship end up undercut. Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, reportedly raised Biden to anger amid genocide in Gaza after the Hamas attacks of 7 October. And yet as Biden’s book was released, the Jerusalem Post reported that a transcript of the two men’s final conversation showed the American president ladling on the praise: “I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through … I still love you, pal … you’re a good man … I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.” To those who lament Biden’s inability or refusal to rein Netanyahu in, it rang depressingly true.

Dealt a tough hand, Biden played it … varyingly. Russia invaded Ukraine. Biden describes how he marshalled support for Kyiv, which he visited in secret, an episode vividly retold. Now, the war is nearly five years old, Trump wants to end it on Russia’s terms, and Biden inexplicably chooses to chastise Volodymyr Zelenskyy for not being “grateful”, an unfortunate echo of Trump and JD Vance attacking the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office. When Biden occupied that space, sitting behind the Resolute Desk (which like all presidents he likes to repeat, to show how, y’know, resolute he is), Biden committed to withdraw from Afghanistan after 20 futile years.

It was the right decision, but the pull-out was botched. Describing his devastation at the deaths of 13 US service members in a suicide bombing in Kabul, Biden skips the furore when, at Dover air force base in Delaware for the dignified transfer of remains, cameras caught him looking at his watch. Grieving parents also said he spoke about Beau more than about their lost children. The ferocity of fire was unfair, some of it partisan for sure, but these were avoidable problems.

Two years have passed. Daily, Trump commits outrages against the decency his predecessor stands for. But Biden’s book comes out in a landscape altered by Democrats’ midterms tsunami. Presidential contenders are starting to jostle. Promise Me, America reads like a message from the old world. Maybe a warning, about mistakes not to be remade. All the way through, the words of another figure from more genteel circles ring clear.

In November 2020, shortly before Biden beat Trump, former British ambassador Kim Darroch told the New Statesman: “What we used to say inside the embassy about Joe Biden – to be indiscreet – was he is certainly past his best and his best was never that great.”

Harsh. But so is history.
news.summary:
New memoir tells of policy feats and battles with Trump but struggles to take responsibility for re-election debacle

Inevitably, readers of Joe Biden’s new memoir will flick forward to find what he says about the events that ended his presidency: increasing pressure about his age and capacity that finally led him to stand aside and anoint Kamala Harris, too late, ushering fascism back to the White House. Alas, Biden thinks he was just fine to keep on serving and the whole thing was a stitch-up by a panicked party.

Of his catastrophic debate in June 2024, when the then 81-year-old president blinked, stuttered and gaped under the lights, Biden writes: “I knew the debate had gone badly. But I knew that debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent presidents. Especially their first ones. I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate, it was my last one.” He raises Barack Obama’s poor performance in his first debate with

news.title: Ultra-Elitist News Website Admits Secretly Paying MAGA Stars
news.text:
Semafor admitted to secretly paying long-time Trump adviser Jason Miller (main picture), former Trump inner-circle member Kellyanne Conway, and a former aide to Kamala Harris, Adrienne Elrod.

The payments came to light after Miller’s eye-popping $15 million income was detailed in court filings, the Post’s report said. 

“In April, the records show, Semafor paid one of Miller’s firms, Scipio Strategic, $100,000 for help booking guests for its World Economy 2026 summit in D.C.,” the report said. 

The event featured members of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Semafor told the Post it paid Miller for “a brief engagement around the event” but did not say which guests Miller helped secure. He was only consulted for that event. 

According to Semafor’s disclosures, Conway and Elrod also helped with that event, and Semafor continues to work with them on other events.

Semafor’s own website touts the publication as “providing audiences with an unparalleled level of journalistic transparency.”

“Transparent News” is one of the three pillars of the new media company, with a rationale for the tagline that claims: “We’re exposing the architecture of our original journalism in an effort to rebuild trust from our audience.”

Semafor was founded by journalist Ben Smith and former Bloomberg CEO Justin B. Smith in 2022 to provide reporting tailor-made for an educated elite. It derives a significant part of its income from special news-related events. 

Semafor, Conway, Miller, and Elrod did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

In a statement to the Post, Meaghan Koppel, Semafor’s global head of communications, wrote: “Like many other media companies, Semafor works with bookers and consultants across the political spectrum to secure speakers for our events. We don’t pay speakers. Both our speakers and guests come for tough, fair, and independent interviews.

“Semafor did not quote Jason Miller or mention him in our Washington coverage during our engagement. We did make two passing references of him in business coverage. We updated those stories with disclosures, and made similar disclosures about our work with Democrat Adrienne Elrod and Republican Kellyanne Conway,” she said. 

The consultants “have no influence on our journalism, online or on our stages,” Semafor co-founder and Editor-in-Chief Ben Smith said in an email to staff, obtained by the Post.

“News organizations don’t always disclose this sort of contract relationship, but we will going forward when we work with consultants who can themselves be the subjects of coverage.”
news.summary:
Michael M. Santiago / Getty ImagesNews outlet Semafor has been forced to admit that it paid D.C. insiders for access to key Washington figures. 

The publication updated 11 articles and newsletters to disclose that it paid political consultants to help secure guests for its events, The Washington Post reported. 

Semafor admitted to secretly paying long-time Trump adviser Jason Miller (main picture), former Trump inner-circle member Kellyanne Conway, and a former aide to Kamala Harris, Adrienne Elrod.

Chay Bowes: The Russian propaganda and disinformation that landed Irish man on an EU blacklist

Once known for exposing Leo Varadkar’s GP contract leak, Bowes is now under EU sanctions.

9.01am, 21 Nov 2026

Share options

Stephen McDermott

IN AUGUST 2024, a short clip circulated online claiming that Reporters Without Borders (RWB) had discovered widespread sympathy for Nazism among Ukrainian soldiers fighting against Russia.

It featured the BBC’s iconic logo in its top-left corner and relayed the story through white captions over grainy images of troops from the front and blurred helmets with SS badges.

As the video cut briskly through grainy frontline stills, its authoritative BBC watermark and crisp white captions seamlessly mimicked a legitimate news dispatch, claiming RWB had uncovered 1,000 cases where combatants had donned Nazi symbols and that the group had called on other media organisations to cover the story. 

But this was not a legitimate BBC report, and RWB never made such a finding.

In a subsequent investigation, the press-freedom group found that the clip was an example of literal fake news promoted by pro-Russian accounts on X and Telegram.

Their report said the video was initially posted by an anonymous account on X called ‘Patricia’, but that one of the first people to pick it up and amplify it was Irishman Chay Bowes.

From there, it went viral across a network of Russian propagandists and the country’s foreign embassies, and was mentioned at a press conference by Maria Zakharova, the official spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry.

Bowes – who first entered the public eye as the whistleblower in the 2020 Leo Varadkar GP contract leak before co-founding The Ditch website – now works for Russian state broadcaster RT and was among 30 individuals sanctioned by the European Union this week.

Announcing the sanctions, the Council of the EU described Bowes and three other media figures as “propagandists”, saying they had participated in information manipulation and spread narratives “that legitimise and sustain” Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Under the measures, Bowes’s EU-based assets are frozen and EU citizens and companies are banned from providing him with funds. He is also prohibited from entering or transiting through EU member states, though this doesn’t include Ireland.

In justifying the sanctions, the council pointed to his work hosting the RT programme “Moscow Mules”,alongside his co-founding of the pro-Russian disinformation network The Islander News.

It also cited his participation in influence operations run by the Wagner Group-founded Foundation to Battle Injustice, as well as his “spreading of anti-Western and anti-Ukraine disinformation” during a 2023 appearance at the UN Security Council on Russia’s behalf.

It said that through these activites, he was “facilitating actions or policies attributable” to the government of Russia which “undermine or threaten democracy, the rule of law, stability or security” in the European Union.

Bowes criticised the move on social media as anti-free speech and an attempt to “bully me into silence”, while People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd-Barrett also labelled it “a sinister development”.

In a brief response to queries from The Journal this week, he said that he considers the sanctions to be “illegal and utterly baseless” and described allegations that he had spread disinformation on behalf of Russian groups as “false”.

Bowes and his defenders have framed the sanctions as an attack on press freedom.

Critics such as People Before Profit have warned that penalising commentators without a trial creates a dangerous slippery slope for free expression, likening it to US sanctions against UN Special Rapporteur for Palestine Francesca Albanese.

The EU though believes its decision is justified following a years-long trail of fabricated stories and Kremlin-aligned disinformation about the war in Ukraine.

Bowes’ journey raises questions about how a figure who first made his name scrutinising Irish politics became such a prolific amplifier of Russian government talking points in the West.

A still from the fake BBC News clipX.com

‘A long line of Irish people queued up to shake his hand’

To understand how a Dublin-born businessman ended up on an EU sanctions list alongside Russian state operatives, it helps to trace a career built on continuous reinvention – one that began not in Russia, but in the Irish medical sector.

Long before Bowes began broadcasting from Moscow, he came into the Irish public’s consciousness as a healthcare entrepreneur turned whistleblower.

In 2017, he co-founded Community Hospital Ireland, a private company that provided healthcare in patients’ homes and reinvested profits into treatment for chronic illness.

The venture brought him into contact with Galway doctor Maitiú Ó Tuathail, then president of the National Association of General Practitioners (NAGP), a now-defunct union for GPs.

The relationship brought NAGP support to CHI, and by 2019, the two were close enough that Ó Tuathail felt comortable sending Bowes a message that showed he had obtained a confidential GP contract between the government and the Irish Medical Organisation.

The young doctor had received a copy of the contract from an acquaintance, then-Taoiseach Leo Varadkar, boasting to Bowes about how he acquired it in a text message: “To be fair, Leo always delivers.”

Leo Varadkar become embroiled in controversy after Chay Bowes revealed he had leaked a GP contractAlamy

Through Web Summit founder Paddy Cosgrave, Bowes teamed up with Village magazine, which published what became known as the ‘Leo the leak’ exposé in 2020 – much of it relying on Bowes’ text messages and documents.

“I was dumbfounded that a friend of the then-Taoiseach was claiming such professional closeness to him that he would improperly forward him potentially explosive confidential documentation,” he told the magazine at the time.

The ensuing political controversy earned Bowes genuine goodwill among a cohort of Irish readers as someone who had helped reveal how the most senior figure in the government did a secret favour for someone in his personal inner circle.

The following year, Cosgrave invited Bowes and Village editor Michael Smith to the stage during the opening of the Web Summit in Lisbon and urged the audience to give them a round of applause.

“@BowesChay spoke on stage at @WebSummit about @LeoVaradkar after which a long line of Irish people queued up to shake his hand,” Cosgrave gushed on Twitter afterwards.

Paddy Cosgrave's tweet about Chay Bowes at the Web SummitX.com / @paddycosgrave

X.com / @paddycosgrave / @paddycosgrave

The episode exposed a combative streak that defined Bowes’s early public life: a readiness to sever personal alliances so that he could challenge institutional power, regardless of the fallout.

The same year as his Web Summit appearance, he parlayed the profile he had attained from his involvement in the ‘Leo the leak’ story by co-founding investigative website The Ditch, alongside journalists Eoghan McNeill and Roman Shortall.

The venture, which initially received financial backing from Cosgrave, cemented his reputation as a relentless, if opportunistic, scrutineer of Irish political power given how many stories they broke about Fine Gael and Fianna Fáil politicians. 

Bowes subsequently resigned as director of and sold his shares in The Ditch in June 2022, before the outlet’s reporting led to the resignations of An Bórd Pleanála deputy chairman Paul Hyde and government junior ministers Damien English and Robert Troy, the latter of whom has since returned to government. 

‘It is simplistic to cast Russia as a deviant nation’

The audience that Bowes built through his role in Ireland’s alternative and independent media between 2020 and 2022 showed his relentless appetite for challenging domestic political orthodoxy.

Soon he began to apply that same contrarian, anti-establishment lens to Western foreign policy.

As the pandemic subsided and Russia prepared to invade Ukraine, the one-time whistleblower’s attention began to shift noticeably to more geopolitical interests.

CNN's homepage on the day Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022Alamy

It was not entirely new ground for Bowes; three years earlier, he had published an essay in the Dublin-based independent magazine Cassandra Voices, taking aim at Nato expansion and criticising EU leaders seeking to absorb Ukraine into the “Western orbit”.

Returning to this theme in January 2022, a month before Russia’s full-scale invasion, he published another essay in which he argued that Ireland – due to its history of partition, ethnic division, and proximity to a powerful neighbour – is uniquely positioned to understand the complexities of the Ukraine-Russia conflict.

He presented the looming conflict through the prism of a crisis rooted in the expansion of Nato and a failure to recognise Russia’s legitimate security interests.

“It is simplistic to cast Russia as a deviant nation hellbent on suppressing and oppressing its neighbours, particularly those previously a part of the Soviet Union,” he wrote.

“The truth is far more complex.”

Yet in February 2022, Bowes’s initial reaction was notably equivocal on what was unfolding at Europe’s eastern border.

When Russia invaded Ukraine in the early hours of 24 February 2022, he took to Twitter to say he didn’t accept the country’s actions or find them acceptable.

His criticism was couched in qualified support for Ukraine (“I am 100% against any action [...] that causes loss of life”) and posts that took as much aim at Nato and the United States as they did at Russia.

Bowes Twitter thread from the morning of 24 February 2022X.com / @BowesChay

X.com / @BowesChay / @BowesChay

There were also times when his criticism of Russia was more categorical.

At one point early in the war, he described what was happening as “immoral” and said that Russia had carried out an “illegal and brutal invasion” that was leading to the “murder” of Ukrainian citizens.

“This entirely unacceptable and unnecessary war in #Ukraine is entirely unjustified and unjustifiable,” he posted.

It was a viewpoint that wasn’t to last.

Over the following year, Bowes’ Twitter feed shifted incrementally from condemning Russia to questioning Western support, moving first through amplification and selective framing rather than fabrication.

In May 2022, he shared a Bloomberg opinion column asking whether then-UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson was prolonging the war; in January 2023, he cited a genuine US State Department human-rights report in a post that argued against funding and arming Kyiv.

Even on 31 August 2022, he still affirmed Ukraine’s right to freedom and statehood, though he did so alongside criticism of Volodymyr Zelenskyy and claims that Kyiv was persecuting Russian speakers in the Donbass region.

Ten months on, appearing via video link at a June 2023 UN Security Council briefing, he had shed all nuance in favour of an unabashedly pro-Kremlin line. 

Invited by Russia, Bowes – given the on-screen title of “scholar specialising in small arms and munitions” - addressed the UN’s highest-authority body and cast Russian troops as “defenders” and Ukraine as a “chaotic and essentially failed state”.

He used his appearance to shift blame for the ongoing bloodshed squarely onto Western capitals.

“Settlement will come, and it is my absolute belief that it is up to those in Washington DC and London, now fuelling the conflict with endless escalatory military aid to Ukraine, to decide where and when that settlement occurs, either at the negotiating table or on the battlefield,” he said.

While Russian ambassador Vassily Nebenzia publicly thanked him afterwards, the next speaker – Soviet-born British historian Sergey Radchenko – rebuked him by name.

Bowes, he said, had come to the UN chamber to lecture delegates on “how terrible it is to support a victim of unprovoked aggression, how terrible it is to help people under attack, how terrible it is to resist imperialist conquest”.

Chay Bowes appears on screen at the UN Security Council in June 2023United Nations

United Nations

Moscow Mules

By tracing Bowes’s odyssey from nuanced early reaction to the war in early 2022 to unambiguous pro-Kremlin, West-critical posturing at the UN 18 months later, one can see how his public pronouncements coincided with his changing professional orbit.

After giving up his work and shares in The Ditch in June 2022, the former whistleblower moved to Moscow in the latter half of that year to become a correspondent for RT.

Even at that stage, the state-funded outlet (previously known as Russia Today) had become an outcast in the broadcasting world on foot of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Brussels sanctioned RT as a state propaganda outlet, and it was banned across the European Union, stripped of its broadcasting licence in the United Kingdom, and blocked from platforms including YouTube, Meta, Google, Apple and TikTok.

But the company gave Bowes an institutional standing and media salary, while also enabling him to continue his anti-establishment talking points against European politicians, the US and Nato.

He was not the first Western figure to take up a role with the broadcaster.

Since the early 2010s, RT has opportunistically recruited Western anti-establishment figures with offers of generous pay and editorial freedom “as a way of authenticating the messaging they want to promote”, according to Stephen Hutchings, professor of Russian studies at the University of Manchester.

Those hired were not necessarily dupes, he explains, but commentators who “saw RT as an opportunity for them to promote their agendas”.

Hutchings notes that the 2022 bans pushed RT into far more overt propaganda, blending contradictions that cast Russia simultaneously as an anti-imperialist champion, a victim of Western cultural colonisation and a great power entitled to its own sphere of influence.

“These three lines don’t really hang together, but that doesn’t matter,” he says.

“You pick whichever of those messages works best for a particular audience or in a particular situation.”

Bowes began his career with RT as a correspondent, appearing in news segments to provide his analysis of global events, in clips that were also shared on social media.

ICYMI: Pentagon Investigates Major Leak Of 'Classified Documents'

Washington is alarmed after a new trove of secret US national security documents relating to Ukraine, China & the Middle East appeared online. 

RT correspondent Chay Bowes is in the studio to explain the events. https://t.co/AQoLHw5WRi— RT_India (@RT_India_news) April 9, 2023

By early 2024, he had been given his own sleekly-edited weekly podcast, Moscow Mules, with targets including EU countries and their leadership, US politics, the Russia-Ukraine war, and domestic affairs in Ireland and the United Kingdom.

Alongside sleek editing, the show adopts a faux-casual, smirking register – using derisive humour as a delivery mechanism to launder hard-edged Kremlin talking points.

A recent episode called ‘The unflushed empire’ examined claims that a foreign power could be behind recent home intrusions targeting 20 members of Finland’s parliament; amid suggestions that the intruders had left behind unflushed toilets and human waste, the episode ironically dismissed the claim by calling it Operation Number Two.

The framing sought to dismiss the story as yet another attempt by the West to blame the Kremlin on even trivial things, a play that helps to undermine criticism of more globally consequential activities by Russia. 

Between these instances of so-called satire, however, have been plenty of cases where Bowes has leaned into Russian disinformation narratives.

In a November 2025 broadcast titled ‘A fool and his money’, the programme suggested that Western financial support for Kyiv is a giant fraud, promising to show how “EU elites and Ukroscammers enjoy revelling in free taxpayer money”.

Framing Western military and financial assistance to Ukraine as an embezzlement scheme is one of the Kremlin’s main anti-Ukraine narratives, designed to turn EU and US citizens against supporting Kyiv and to derail the country’s EU accession.

In another episode from August, Bowes appeared on-screen beside an article from a website called the Irish Sun, reporting corruption allegations involving Zelenskyy’s staff.

Despite its name, the site is an online outlet operated by an Australian company, Midwest Radio Network, on behalf of its Dubai-based parent company, Big News Network.

It was set up in 2002 and claims to take its name from a newspaper that was published in Ireland from 1880, and explicitly disclaims any connection to the Murdoch-owned newspaper of the same name.

“Irish Sun is not associated with The Sun in the UK, or that publication’s Irish edition,” its ‘about page’ says.

Big News Network, which supplies the site’s syndicated content, is an international syndication network identified by disinformation researchers as a “pink slime” operation that republishes sanctioned Russian state media. 

The Irish Sun article used by Bowes visibly credited RT.com, allowing the segment to function like a digital hall of mirrors.

Kremlin-aligned copy left Moscow via RT, passed through an Australian-owned aggregator donning an Irish masthead, and bounced straight back onto Bowes’s studio screen in Russia as apparent third-party corroboration.

Advertisement

Source: RT.com

The show has also repeatedly pushed the pretext for Russia’s invasion by claiming that Ukrainian state bodies are partnering with neo-Nazis and that Volodymyr Zelenskyy is an “unelected dictator” presiding over a corrupt regime.

Ukrainian volunteer militias with far-right roots like the Azov Battalion were once active in the country, but were formally absorbed into the country’s regular military structure over a decade ago.

While far-right elements persist within pockets of the armed forces, researchers note they remain a small minority rather than a state-controlling force, with one calling them a “proverbial drop in the ocean”.

Zelenskyy remains in office because Ukrainian law prohibits holding elections under martial law during a foreign invasion.

It’s an arrangement that has occasionally prompted debate inside Ukraine, but has been navigated through constitutional consensus, regular parliamentary votes, and the view that a ballot must wait until peacetime.

One episode description recently labelled Zelenskyy as the “Cocainefuhrer”, linking the claim that he is an unelected Nazi to an ongoing smear by Russia that the Ukrainian leader is a drug addict.

The misinformation spread on Moscow Mules is not just limited to the conflict in Ukraine.

In the same October 2026 episode mocking the Finnish break-ins, an episode description claimed that Met Police in London had been “traded for Sharia patrols”, reviving a long-debunked far-right trope that suggests that parts of the British capital have ceded control of their streets to Islamic religious police.

“What you definitely can’t do is drink a beer near a mosque because, of course, Islam is the national religion of the UK now,” he told viewers, introducing a clip taken from social media where a man asks a group not to consume alcohol on a street.

“Imagine a white British Christian went and complained about this type of stuff that’s also happening in the UK right now; think about what would happen [...] Six months in prison? Hate crime? Racism? Nazi? You get the picture.”

Another episode criticised USAID as US taxpayer money going “down the drain of the clogged bathrooms of transgender Colombian operas”.

It echoed a White House and DOGE talking point that cited a purported “$47,000 (€43,000) grant for a ‘transgender opera’ in Colombia” as proof of “waste and abuse” to justify dismantling USAID, though spending records show USAID gave no money to the project.

Elon Musk wearing a DOGE baseball cap in the White HouseAlamy

The Islander News

When EU bans at the outset of the war cut RT off from the European airwaves, Moscow’s messaging apparatus required a more ostensibly independent vehicle to reach Western readers.

Bowes helped to fill this gap through The Islander News, another website he founded in recent years.

His involvement in the project served as a key justification for his recent sanctioning by the EU council.

The legal text of the council’s decision specifically highlighted his work on the outlet, which bills itself as offering “deep geopolitical analysis” and “long-form op-eds” aimed at a “more just world order” on Telegram and Substack.

Like Moscow Mules, The Islander’s primary focus is anti-Western, Kremlin-aligned commentary.

It targets Ukraine and EU institutions, and has also sought to undermine elections in countries on Russia’s periphery.

During contested elections in Georgia and Moldova last year, Bowes framed pro-democracy protests in Tbilisi as an attempted “coup”, while The Islander also amplified unsubstantiated claims of voter suppression and warmongering against Moldova’s pro-EU government.

Bowes criticising Moldova in similar terms to his criticism of UkraineX.com

The outlet has also come under fire for its stance on the invasion of Ukraine, particularly through its laundering and amplification of narratives pushed by Storm-1516, a Russian-affiliated disinformation and influence operation.

In May last year, a report by Vignium – France’s state agency tasked with detecting foreign digital interference – found that the “vast majority” of Storm-1516 narratives were amplified by social media accounts and websites belonging to four named individuals.

One of those individuals was Bowes, with the report including his handle on X and the URL of The Islander featuring alongside his name.

The report said that The Islander was “considered likely to have been paid for or activated by” malicious actors within the Russian information manipulation sector.

“Vignium notes that most of these actors have close links with Russian organisations with a long history of information operations targeting foreign audiences,” the report says.

One of the Storm-1516 narratives identified by Vignium was a false claim from November 2023 that Zelenskyy had bought two luxury yachts worth $75 million (€68 million).

Debunking the story, the Associated Press established that both yachts remained for sale and that the purported sales documents contained outdated branding, and specifically named the Islander as publishing the claim. 

Another report by Clemson University in South Carolina also found that Bowes had, through The Islander, shared multiple narratives from Storm-1516 and the Foundation to Battle Injustice, a second Russian disinformation and influence operation founded by the since-deceased Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin.

Wagner Group founder Yevgeny PrigozhinAlamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

Russian influence campaigns rely on ostensibly independent sites and trusted Western commentators to give fabricated stories “the appearance of legitimacy” and reach audiences predisposed to believe them, explains Darren Linvill, co-director of Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub.

Disinformation experts call this process information laundering, a tactic in which state-backed propaganda is routed through seemingly independent third-party outlets to obscure its origins, before appearing to Western audiences as credible news.

Between 2023 and 2024, Linvill says, Bowes’s routine sharing of Storm-1516 claims across The Islander and social media made him, for a time, “Russia’s leading mouthpiece in sharing this set of lies”.

Bowes has said that he is no longer involved in The Islander.

It is reported that he gave control of the project to Nolan in the first half of 2024, a timeline consistent with the fact that The Islander’s newer X account (created in July 2024) lists Nolan as its sole owner.

Even with that shift in ownership, Brussels’ citing of both RT and The Islander in its 16 November decision to sanction Bowes highlights their distinct roles in his wider output.

Although RT operates as a heavily branded, state-stamped broadcast studio, which had been locked out of European airwaves, The Islander worked as a more shadowy operation.

By presenting itself as an independent Anglophone outlet, it managed to dress Kremlin up as impartial commentary to slip past sceptical Western readers on Telegram and Substack.

Ten narratives on X

Bowes continued to post similar claims on his personal channels, so articles and posts published under The Islander’s banner after the transfer of ownership in 2024 cannot be attributed to him.

That didn’t stop him from amplifying Storm-1516 elsewhere, particularly through his account on X.

An analysis by The Journal of his posts on the social media platform found that he promoted at least 10 other narratives identified by Vignium as originating from the group.

Several echoed the same formula as the yacht rumour, alleging extravagant purchases by Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife.

In October 2023, Bowes shared a now-deleted post – preserved in an online forum archive – referencing fabricated claims that Olena Zelenska had spent over $1 million (€910,000) at Cartier.

Over the following year and a half, he also helped circulate bogus stories that the Zelenskyys had bought a luxury Bugatti, Sting’s Tuscan estate, France’s Milleis bank, and – according to researchers tracking German election interference – Hitler’s Eagle’s Nest retreat.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a frequent target of BowesAlamy

Bowes did not always present such claims as established fact.

He openly noted that documents in a post regarding Milleis bank – subsequently debunked by AFP – were uncertain or “unverified”.

“A French video is circulating alleging Zelenskys offshore company was involved in buying a French Bank,” he said on X.

“The unverified report says Milleis Banque was bought via his offshore Co. Maltex for approx €1.2B.”

Other posts targeted high-profile figures and major international events.

In early 2024, he promoted a fabricated story of a Ukrainian plot to assassinate Tucker Carlson, before sharing a smear falsely claiming Russian opposition figure Leonid Volkov was attacked by a former lover.

That July, a post amplifying a fake Hamas threat against the Paris Olympics racked up nearly three million views.

Storm-1516’s Western election narratives also featured prominently on Bowes’ X feed.

Ahead of the US presidential election in October 2024, he shared a fabricated claim accusing Kamala Harris of cocaine addiction.

Months later, during Germany’s federal election, he circulated a staged video falsely purporting to show postal ballots for the far-right AfD being shredded.

That pattern continued between May and July 2025 during an influence push targeting Moldova.

In surviving posts later mapped by researchers, Bowes promote an allegation traced back to the Foundation to Battle Injustice via the fringe outlet Veterans Today.

His focus on European ballots also drew direct pushback inside the EU in May 2025, when Romanian authorities detained Bowes and denied him entry after he flew in from Dublin ahead of a controversial re-run of the country’s presidential election.

He was declared a “threat to the security of the state”, and subsequently boarded a flight to Istanbul.

Nor do his posts simply concern direct Russian interests.

In another study, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue identified Bowes as a frequent commentator on immigration in Ireland in ways that echo claims by Russian state media.

His posts included descriptions of immigration as a “scam” and critiques of the Irish government for giving housing and financial support to Ukrainian refugees, alongside claims that the Ukrainian government was a “corrupted dictatorship”.

“While of course entitled to his personal opinions, it is interesting given his employment as an RT commentator that he selectively framed the Ukrainian government in terms aligning with Kremlin narratives,” the report said.

“With over 270,000 followers on X, his content is available to Irish audiences but is also frequently shared by other actors in pro-Kremlin online spaces.”

An anti-immigration protest in Dublin in 2024Alamy

Ciaran O’Connor, a senior analyst at the ISD, points out that Bowes – who recently labelled the EU “an authoritarian network of client states where sovereignty is a memory” – frequently frames migration as an EU-enforced “scam” imposed on Ireland from outside.

According to O’Connor, Bowes also taps into deeply felt domestic grievances in Ireland over housing, immigration and the cost of living in a manner that acts as a “gateway”.

He says this can build trust with local audiences who view Bowes as an independent voice, before gradually introducing them to Kremlin-aligned commentary on Russia and Ukraine they might never have sought out on their own.

Bowes has denied being associated with an influence operation or being paid to post material sympathetic to Russian views.

Clemson University’s Darren Linvill says there is a distinction between active state direction and willing amplification, noting he has seen no evidence that Bowes orchestrated Russian influence campaigns himself.

“I think the evidence points to him being a useful mouthpiece, not a mastermind,” he says.

Bowes has removed posts that contain misinformation, as he did with the fake BBC clip about Ukrainian Nazis once he was contacted by RSF.

‘No evidence, no hearing’

Eventually, Brussels decided that Bowes had crossed the line from contrarian commentator to active conduit for foreign interference.

The extensive trail of digital amplification landed him on the European Council’s sanctions list this week.

In its announcement, the council said the decision to target Bowes came amid the backdrop of “increasing Russian hybrid activities aimed at destabilising EU societies”. 

The move triggered severe practical consequences for Bowes, leading to his assets being frozen across the EU and a strict ban on EU citizens or entities providing him with funds.

The measures do not prevent him from returning to Ireland, but they effectively quarantine his financial and professional footprint within the EU.

Bowes has aggressively framed the move as an attack on fundamental rights, casting the sanctions as an authoritarian attempt to silence dissenting voices.

“The EU sanctioned me for being a ‘disinformation hub’,” he wrote on X afterwards.

“No evidence, no hearing, nothing. Now I can’t move around the EU, can’t bank, and can’t receive money. All because I challenged the Western narrative on Ukraine.”

Others rowed in to defend him, including former Independents4Change MEP Clare Daly, who described the sanctions as “extrajudicial punishment for disfavoured speech”, and the aforementioned TD Richard Boyd-Barrett, who claimed they were issued to a “journalist for not toeing [the] western line”.

People Before Profit TD Richard Boyd-BarrettAlamy

Their defence taps into a vital democratic question about an individual’s right to challenge prevailing orthodoxy.

But the documented trail of interference at such a heightened time would also lead to questions if Brussels didn’t act.

The council’s legal text surgically cited Bowes’ active involvement in “information manipulation” and his role as a key amplifier for operations like Storm-1516.

The threshold for sanctions was deemed to have been crossed not when Bowes voiced pro-Kremlin views, but when his commentary became, in the opinion of the European Council, a documented conduit for malicious foreign interference.

Bowes has framed the move as censorship, arguing on X that he was sanctioned without a hearing or evidence merely for offering “dissenting opinions”.

Gavin Barrett, professor of EU constitutional and economic law at University College Dublin’s Sutherland School of Law, notes that while EU measures must be legally reasoned, Bowes can challenge his listing before the EU courts in Luxembourg under Article 263 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

Any such challenge would likely invoke Article 11 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, which protects freedom of expression and media pluralism.

Yet Barrett notes that judges would weigh that protection against “times of massive media manipulation”, scrutinising his role at banned state broadcaster RT alongside posts sharing a fake BBC clip and a staged German ballot-shredding video.

“A court might well take the view that this kind of activity is far removed from the kind of legitimate journalistic activity intended to be protected by the Charter,” he says.
